Was it to amuse her? was it to ensnare her? was it to banter her? or was there something substantial and weighty in it? But, of all the thoughts she had as to <hi type="italic">what manner of salutation it should be,</hi> I believe she had not the least idea of its being ever intended or used for a prayer, as it is, and has been, for many ages, by the corrupt, degenerate, and anti-christian ages of the church, and to be ten times repeated for the Lord's prayer once; so it is in the church of Rome. But her thoughtfulness upon this occasion gives a very useful intimation to young people of her sex, when addresses are made to them, to consider and <hi type="italic">cast in their minds</hi> what manner of <hi type="italic">salutations</hi> they are, whence they come, and what their tendency is, that they may receive them accordingly, and may always <hi type="italic">stand on their guard.</hi> <div eID="gen25143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25144" type="x-p"/> IV. The message itself which the angel had to deliver to her. Some time the angel gives her to <hi type="italic">pause;</hi> but, observing that this did but increase her perplexity, he went on with his errand, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.30">v. 30</reference>. To what he had said she made no reply; he therefore confirms it: "<hi type="italic">Fear not, Mary,</hi> I have no other design than to assure thee that <hi type="italic">thou hast found favour with God</hi> more than thou thinkest of, as there are many who think they are more favoured with God than they really are." Note, Those that have <hi type="italic">found favour with God</hi> should not give way to disquieting distrustful fears. Doth God favour thee? Fear not, though the world frown upon thee. Is he for thee? No matter who is against thee. <div eID="gen25144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25145" type="x-p"/> 1. Though she is a <hi type="italic">virgin,</hi> she shall have the honour of being a <hi type="italic">mother:</hi> "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son,</hi> and thou shalt have the naming of him; thou shalt <hi type="italic">call his name Jesus,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.1.31">v. 31</reference>. It was the sentence upon Eve, that, though she should have the honour to be the <hi type="italic">mother of all living,</hi> yet this mortification shall be an allay to that honour, that <hi type="italic">her desire shall be to her husband,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">shall rule over her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen. iii. 16</reference>. But Mary has the honour without the allay. <div eID="gen25145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25146" type="x-p"/> 2. Though she lives in <hi type="italic">poverty</hi> and <hi type="italic">obscurity,</hi> yet she shall have the honour to be the mother of the Messiah; her son shall be named <hi type="italic">Jesus—a Saviour,</hi> such a one as the world <hi type="italic">needs,</hi> rather than such one as the Jews <hi type="italic">expect.</hi> <div eID="gen25146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25147" type="x-p"/> (1.) He will be very <hi type="italic">nearly allied</hi> to the <hi type="italic">upper world.</hi> He <hi type="italic">shall be great,</hi> truly great, incontestably great; for he shall be called <hi type="italic">the Son of the Highest,</hi> the Son of God who is <hi type="italic">the Highest;</hi> of the same nature, as the son is of the same nature with the father; and very dear to him, as the son is to the father. He shall be <hi type="italic">called,</hi> and not <hi type="italic">miscalled,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Son of the Highest;</hi> for he is himself <hi type="italic">God over all, blessed for evermore,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Rom. ix. 5</reference>. Note, Those who are the children of God, though but by adoption and regeneration, are <hi type="italic">truly great,</hi> and therefore are concerned to be <hi type="italic">very good,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.1-1John.3.2">1 John iii. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen25147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25148" type="x-p"/> (2.) He will be very <hi type="italic">highly preferred</hi> in the <hi type="italic">lower world;</hi> for, though born under the most disadvantageous circumstances possible, and appearing in the form of a servant, yet <hi type="italic">the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">v. 32</reference>. He puts her in mind that she was <hi type="italic">of the house of David;</hi> and that therefore, since neither the <hi type="italic">Salique law,</hi> nor the right of primogeniture, took place in the entail of his throne, it was not impossible but that she might bring forth an heir to it, and therefore might the more easily <hi type="italic">believe</hi> it when she was told by an angel from heaven that she <hi type="italic">should</hi> do so, that after the sceptre had been long <hi type="italic">departed</hi> from that ancient and honourable family it should now at length return to it again, to remain in it, not by succession, but in the same hand to eternity. His people will not <hi type="italic">give him that throne,</hi> will not acknowledge his right to <hi type="italic">rule them;</hi> but the <hi type="italic">Lord God</hi> shall give him a right to <hi type="italic">rule them,</hi> and set him as <hi type="italic">his king</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">holy hill of Zion.</hi> He assures her, [1.] That his kingdom shall be <hi type="italic">spiritual:</hi> he shall <hi type="italic">reign over the house of Jacob,</hi> not <hi type="italic">Israel according to the flesh,</hi> for they neither came into his interests nor did they continue long a people; it must therefore be a <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> kingdom, the house of Israel <hi type="italic">according to the promise,</hi> that he must <hi type="italic">rule over.</hi> [2.] That it shall be eternal: he shall reign <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> and <hi type="italic">of his kingdom there shall be no end,</hi> as there had been long since of the temporal reign of David's house, and would shortly be of the state of Israel. Other crowns endure not <hi type="italic">to every generation,</hi> but Christ's doth, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Prov. xxvii. 24</reference>. The gospel is the <hi type="italic">last</hi> dispensation, we are to look for no other. <div eID="gen25148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25149" type="x-p"/> V. The further information given her, upon her enquiry concerning the birth of this prince. <div eID="gen25149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25150" type="x-p"/> 1. It is a just enquiry which she makes: "<hi type="italic">How shall this be?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.34">v. 34</reference>. How can I now presently conceive a child" (for so the angel meant) "when I <hi type="italic">know not a man;</hi> must it therefore be otherwise than by ordinary generation? If so, let me now <hi type="italic">how?</hi>" She knew that the Messiah must be born of <hi type="italic">a virgin;</hi> and, if she must be his mother, she desires to know how. This was not the language of her distrust, or any doubt of what the angel said, but of a desire to be further instructed. <div eID="gen25150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25151" type="x-p"/> 2. It is a satisfactory answer that is given to it, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.35">v. 35</reference>. (1.) She shall conceive by <hi type="italic">the power of the Holy Ghost,</hi> whose proper work and office is to <hi type="italic">sanctify,</hi> and therefore to sanctify the virgin for this purpose. The Holy Ghost is called the <hi type="italic">power of the Highest.</hi> Doth she ask how this shall be? This is enough to help her over all the difficulty there appears in it; a divine power will undertake it, not the power of an angel employed in it, as in other works of wonder, but the power of <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost</hi> himself. <div eID="gen25151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25152" type="x-p"/> (2.) She must <hi type="italic">ask no questions</hi> concerning the way and manner how it shall be wrought; for the Holy Ghost, as the <hi type="italic">power of the Highest,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">overshadow</hi> her, as the <hi type="italic">cloud</hi> covered the tabernacle when the glory of God took possession of it, to conceal it from those that would too curiously observe the motions of it, and pry into the mystery of it. The formation of every babe in the womb, and the entrance of the spirit of life into it, is a mystery in nature; none knows <hi type="italic">the way of the spirit, nor how the bones are formed in the womb of her that is with child,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Eccl. xi. 5</reference>. We were <hi type="italic">made in secret,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15-Ps.139.16">Ps. cxxxix. 15, 16</reference>. Much more was the formation of the child Jesus a <hi type="italic">mystery;</hi> without controversy, <hi type="italic">great was the mystery of godliness, God manifest in the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. iii. 16</reference>. It is a <hi type="italic">new thing created in the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.22">Jer. xxxi. 22</reference>), concerning which we must not covet to be <hi type="italic">wise above what is written.</hi> <div eID="gen25152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25153" type="x-p"/> (3.) The child she shall conceive is a <hi type="italic">holy thing,</hi> and therefore must not be conceived by <hi type="italic">ordinary generation,</hi> because he must not share in the common corruption and pollution of the human nature. He is spoken of emphatically, <hi type="italic">That Holy Thing,</hi> such as never was; and he shall be called <hi type="italic">the Son of God,</hi> as the Son of the Father by eternal generation, as an indication of which he shall now be formed by the Holy Ghost in the present conception. His human nature must be so produced, as it was fit that should be which was to be taken into union with the divine nature. <div eID="gen25153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25154" type="x-p"/> 3. It was a further encouragement to her faith to be told that <hi type="italic">her cousin Elisabeth,</hi> though stricken in years, was <hi type="italic">with child,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.36">v. 36</reference>. Here is an age of wonders beginning, and therefore be not surprised: here is one among thy own relations truly great, though not altogether so great as this; it is usual with God to advance in working wonders. <hi type="italic">Greater works than these shall ye do.</hi> Though Elisabeth was, on the father's side, of the <hi type="italic">daughters of Aaron</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.5">v. 5</reference>), yet on the mother's side she might be of the house of David, for those two families often intermarried, as an earnest of the uniting of the royalty and the priesthood of the Messiah. <hi type="italic">This is the sixth month with her that was called barren.</hi> This intimates, as Dr. Lightfoot thinks, that all the instances in the Old Testament of those having children that had been long barren, which was above nature, were designed to prepare the world for the belief of a virgin's bearing a son, which was against nature. And therefore, even in the birth of Isaac, Abraham saw Christ's day, foresaw such a miracle in the birth of Christ. The angel assures Mary of this, to encourage her faith, and concludes with that great truth, of undoubted certainty and universal use, <hi type="italic">For with God nothing shall be impossible</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.37">v. 37</reference>), and, if nothing, then not this. Abraham therefore staggered not at the belief of the divine promise, because he was strong in his belief of the divine power, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.20-Rom.4.21">Rom. iv. 20, 21</reference>. No <hi type="italic">word</hi> of God must be <hi type="italic">incredible to us,</hi> as long as no <hi type="italic">work</hi> of God is <hi type="italic">impossible to him.</hi> <div eID="gen25154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25155" type="x-p"/> VI. Her acquiescence in the will of God concerning her, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.38">v. 38</reference>. She owns herself, 1. A believing subject to the divine authority: "<hi type="italic">Behold, the handmaid of the Lord.</hi> Lord, I am at thy service, at thy disposal, to do what thou commandest me." She objects not the danger of spoiling her marriage, and blemishing her reputation, but leaves the issue with God, and submits entirely to his will. 2. A believing expectant of the divine favour. She is not only content that it should be so, but humbly desires that it may be so: <hi type="italic">Be it unto me according to thy word.</hi> Such a favour as this it was not for her to slight, or be indifferent to; and for what God has <hi type="italic">promised</hi> he will be <hi type="italic">sought unto;</hi> by prayer we must put our <hi type="italic">amen,</hi> or <hi type="italic">so be it,</hi> to the promise. <hi type="italic">Remember,</hi> and perform <hi type="italic">thy word unto thy servant, upon which thou has caused me to hope.</hi> We must, as Mary here, <hi type="italic">guide</hi> our desires by the word of God, and <hi type="italic">ground</hi> our hopes <hi type="italic">upon</hi> it. Be it unto me <hi type="italic">according to thy word;</hi> just so, and no otherwise. <div eID="gen25155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25156" type="x-p"/> Hereupon, <hi type="italic">the angel departed from her;</hi> having completed the errand he was sent upon, he returned, to give an account of it, and receive new instructions. Converse with angels was always a transient thing, and soon over; it will be constant and permanent in the future state. It is generally supposed that just at this instant the virgin <hi type="italic">conceived,</hi> by the <hi type="italic">overshadowing power</hi> of the Holy Ghost: but, the scripture being decently silent concerning it, it doth not become us to be <hi type="italic">inquisitive,</hi> much less <hi type="italic">positive.</hi>
entries.bec2b2aee9a51ad861144d0f79319b50b66d4493: <div eID="gen25156" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Interview of Mary and Elisabeth; The Song of Mary.</title> <div sID="gen25157" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">39</hi> And Mary arose in those days, and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Juda; <hi type="super">40</hi> And entered into the house of Zacharias, and saluted Elisabeth. <hi type="super">41</hi> And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost: <hi type="super">42</hi> And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou among women, and blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the fruit of thy womb. <hi type="super">43</hi> And whence <hi type="italic">is</hi> this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? <hi type="super">44</hi> For, lo, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy. <hi type="super">45</hi> And blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord. <hi type="super">46</hi> And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord, <hi type="super">47</hi> And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour. <hi type="super">48</hi> For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed. <hi type="super">49</hi> For he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name. <hi type="super">50</hi> And his mercy <hi type="italic">is</hi> on them that fear him from generation to generation. 51 He hath showed strength with his arm; he hath scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. <hi type="super">52</hi> He hath put down the mighty from <hi type="italic">their</hi> seats, and exalted them of low degree. <hi type="super">53</hi> He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away. <hi type="super">54</hi> He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of <hi type="italic">his</hi> mercy; <hi type="super">55</hi> As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever. <hi type="super">56</hi> And Mary abode with her about three months, and returned to her own house. <div eID="gen25157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25158" type="x-p"/> We have here an interview between the two happy mothers, Elisabeth and Mary: the angel, by intimating to Mary the favour bestowed on her cousin Elisabeth (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.36">v. 36</reference>), gave occasion for it; and sometimes it may prove a better piece of service that we think to bring good people together, to compare notes. Here is, <div eID="gen25158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25159" type="x-p"/> I. The visit which Mary made to Elisabeth. Mary was the <hi type="italic">younger,</hi> and younger with child; and therefore, if they must come together, it was fittest that Mary should take the journey, not insisting on the preference which the greater dignity of her conception gave her, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.39">v. 39</reference>. She <hi type="italic">arose,</hi> and left her affairs, to attend this greater matter: <hi type="italic">in those days, at that time</hi> (as it is commonly explained, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">Jer. xxxiii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.4">l. 4</reference>), in a day or two after the angel had visited her, taking some time first, as it is supposed, for her devotion, or rather hastening away to her cousin's, where she would have more leisure, and better help, in the family of a priest. She went, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">meta spoudes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">with care, diligence,</hi> and <hi type="italic">expedition;</hi> not as young people commonly go abroad and visit their friends, to <hi type="italic">divert</hi> herself, but to <hi type="italic">inform</hi> herself: she went <hi type="italic">to a city of Judah in the hill-country;</hi> it is not named, but by comparing the description of it here with <reference osisRef="Josh.21.10-Josh.21.11">Josh. xxi. 10, 11</reference>, it appears to be <hi type="italic">Hebron,</hi> for that is there said to be <hi type="italic">in the hill-country of Judah,</hi> and to belong to the priests, the sons of Aaron; thither Mary hastened, though it was a long journey, some scores of miles. <div eID="gen25159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25160" type="x-p"/> 1. Dr. Lightfoot offers a conjecture that she was to <hi type="italic">conceive</hi> our Saviour there at Hebron, and perhaps had so much intimated to her by the angel, or some other way; and therefore she made such haste thither. He thinks it probable that Shiloh, of the tribe of Judah, and the seed of David, should be <hi type="italic">conceived</hi> in a city of Judah and of David, as he was to be born in Bethlehem, another city which belonged to them both. In Hebron the promise was given to Isaac, circumcision was instituted. Here (saith he) Abraham had his first land, and David his first crown: here lay interred the three couples, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah, and, as antiquity has held, Adam and Eve. He therefore thinks that it suits singularly with the harmony and consent which God uses in his works that the promise should begin to take place by the conception of the Messias, even among those patriarchs to whom it was given. I see no improbability in the conjecture, but add this for the support of it, that Elisabeth said (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.45">v. 45</reference>), <hi type="italic">There shall be a performance;</hi> as if it were not performed yet, but was to be performed there. <div eID="gen25160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25161" type="x-p"/> 2. It is generally supposed that she went thither for the confirming of her faith by the sign which the angel had given her, her cousin's being with child, and to rejoice with her sister-favourite. And, besides, she went thither, perhaps, that she might be more retired from company, or else might have more agreeable company than she could have in Nazareth. We may suppose that she did not acquaint any of her neighbours at Nazareth with the message she had received from heaven, yet longed to <hi type="italic">talk over</hi> a thing she had a thousand time <hi type="italic">thought over,</hi> and knew no person in the world with whom she could <hi type="italic">freely</hi> converse concerning it but her cousin Elisabeth, and therefore she hastened to her. Note, it is very beneficial and comfortable for those that have a good work of grace begun in their souls, and Christ in the <hi type="italic">forming</hi> there, to consult those who are in the same case, that they may communicate experiences one to another; and they will find that, as in water face answers to face, so doth the heart of man to man, of Christian to Christian. <div eID="gen25161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25162" type="x-p"/> II. The meeting between Mary and Elisabeth. Mary entered into the house of Zacharias; but he, being <hi type="italic">dumb</hi> and <hi type="italic">deaf,</hi> kept his chamber, it is probable, and saw no company; and therefore she <hi type="italic">saluted Elisabeth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.40">v. 40</reference>), told her she was come to make her a visit, to know her state, and <hi type="italic">rejoice with her</hi> in her joy. <div eID="gen25162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25163" type="x-p"/> Now, at their first coming together, for the confirmation of the faith of both of them, there was something very extraordinary. Mary knew that Elisabeth was with child, but it does not appear that Elisabeth had been told any thing of her cousin Mary's being designed for the mother of the Messiah; and therefore what knowledge she appears to have had of it must have come by a <hi type="italic">revelation,</hi> which would be a great encouragement to Mary. <div eID="gen25163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25164" type="x-p"/> 1. The babe <hi type="italic">leaped in her womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.41">v. 41</reference>. It is very probable that she had been several weeks <hi type="italic">quick</hi> (for she was six months gone), and that she had often felt the child stir; but this was a more than ordinary motion of the child, which alarmed her to expect something very extraordinary, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eskirtese</hi></hi>. It is the same word that is used by the LXX. (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.22">Gen. xxv. 22</reference>) for the <hi type="italic">struggling</hi> of Jacob and Esau in Rebecca's womb, and the mountains <hi type="italic">skipping,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">Ps. cxiv. 4</reference>. The <hi type="italic">babe leaped</hi> as it were to give a signal to his mother that <hi type="italic">he</hi> was now at had whose forerunner he was to be, about six months in ministry, as he was in being; or, it was the effect of some strong impression made upon the mother. Now began to be fulfilled what the angel said to his father (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.15">v. 15</reference>), that he should be <hi type="italic">filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother's womb;</hi> and perhaps he himself had some reference to this, when he said (<reference osisRef="John.3.29">John iii. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">The friend of the Bridegroom rejoiceth greatly, because of the Bridegroom's voice,</hi> heard, though not by him, yet by his mother. <div eID="gen25164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25165" type="x-p"/> 2. Elisabeth was herself <hi type="italic">filled with the Holy Ghost,</hi> or a Spirit of prophecy, by which, as well as by the particular suggestions of the Holy Ghost she was filled with, she was given to understand that the Messiah was at hand, in whom prophecy should revive, and by whom the Holy Ghost should be more plentifully poured out than ever, according to the expectations of those who <hi type="italic">waited for the consolation of Israel.</hi> The uncommon motion of the babe in her womb was a token of extraordinary emotion of her spirit under a divine impulse. Note, Those whom Christ graciously visits may know it by their being <hi type="italic">filled with the Holy Ghost;</hi> for, <hi type="italic">if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.</hi> <div eID="gen25165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25166" type="x-p"/> III. The welcome which Elisabeth, by the Spirit of prophecy, gave to Mary, the mother of our Lord; not as to a common friend making a common visit, but as to one of whom the Messiah was to be born. <div eID="gen25166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25167" type="x-p"/> 1. She congratulates her on her honour, and, though perhaps she knew not of it till <hi type="italic">just now,</hi> she acknowledges it with the greatest assurance and satisfaction. She <hi type="italic">spoke with a loud voice,</hi> which does not at all intimate (as some think) that there was a floor or a wall between them, but that she was in a transport or exultation of joy, and said what she cared not who knew. She said, <hi type="italic">Blessed art thou among women,</hi> the same word that the angels had said (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.28">v. 28</reference>); for thus this will of God, concerning honouring the Son, should be done <hi type="italic">on earth</hi> as it is <hi type="italic">done in heaven.</hi> But Elisabeth adds a reason, <hi type="italic">Therefore blessed art thou</hi> because <hi type="italic">blessed is the fruit of thy womb;</hi> thence it was that she derived this excelling dignity. Elisabeth was the wife of a priest, and in years, yet she <hi type="italic">grudges</hi> not that her kinswoman, who was many years younger than she, and every way her inferior, should have the honour of conceiving in her virginity, and being the mother of the Messiah, whereas the honour put upon her was <hi type="italic">much less;</hi> she <hi type="italic">rejoices</hi> in it, and is well pleased, as her son was afterwards, that she who <hi type="italic">cometh after her is preferred before her,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.27">John i. 27</reference>. Note, While we cannot but own that we are more <hi type="italic">favoured</hi> of God than we deserve, let us by no means envy that others are <hi type="italic">more highly</hi> favoured than we are. <div eID="gen25167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25168" type="x-p"/> 2. She acknowledges her condescension, in making her this visit (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?</hi> Observe, (1.) She calls the virgin Mary the <hi type="italic">mother of her Lord</hi> (as David in spirit, called the Messiah Lord, <hi type="italic">his Lord</hi>), for she knew he was to be <hi type="italic">Lord of all.</hi> (2.) She not only bids her welcome to her house, though perhaps she came in mean circumstances, but reckons this visit a great favour, which she thought herself unworthy of. <hi type="italic">Whence is this to me?</hi> It is in reality, and not in compliment, that she saith, "This was a greater favour than I could have expected." Note, Those that are filled with the Holy Ghost have <hi type="italic">low thoughts</hi> of their own merits, and high thoughts of God's favours. Her son the Baptist spoke to the same purport with this, when he said, <hi type="italic">Comest thou to me?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.3.14">Matt. iii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen25168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25169" type="x-p"/> 3. She acquaints her with the concurrence of the babe in her womb, in this welcome to her (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.44">v. 44</reference>): "Thou certainly bringest some extraordinary tidings, some extraordinary blessing, with thee; for <hi type="italic">as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in my ears,</hi> not only my heart <hi type="italic">leaped for joy,</hi> though I knew not immediately why or wherefore, but the <hi type="italic">babe in my womb,</hi> who was not capable of knowing, <hi type="italic">did so</hi> too." He <hi type="italic">leaped</hi> as it were <hi type="italic">for joy</hi> that the Messiah, whose harbinger he was to be, would himself come soon after him. This would serve very much to strengthen the faith of the virgin, that there were such assurances as these given to others; and it would be in part the accomplishment of what had been so often foretold, that there should be <hi type="italic">universal joy before the Lord, when he cometh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.98.8-Ps.98.9">Ps. xcviii. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen25169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25170" type="x-p"/> 4. She commends her faith, and encourages it (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.45">v. 45</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed is she that believed.</hi> Believing souls are blessed souls, and will be found so at last; this blessedness cometh <hi type="italic">through faith,</hi> even the blessedness of being related to Christ, and having him <hi type="italic">formed in the soul.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> who <hi type="italic">believe</hi> the word of God, for that Word will not fail them; <hi type="italic">there shall,</hi> without doubt, <hi type="italic">be a performance of those things which are told her from the Lord.</hi> Note, The inviolable certainty of the promise is the undoubted felicity of those that build upon it and expect their all from it. The faithfulness of God is the blessedness of the faith of the saints. Those that have experienced the performance of God's promises themselves should encourage others to hope that he will be as good as his word to them also: <hi type="italic">I will tell you what God has done for my soul.</hi> <div eID="gen25170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25171" type="x-p"/> IV. Mary's song of praise, upon this occasion. Elisabeth's prophecy was an echo to the virgin Mary's salutation, and this song is yet a stronger <hi type="italic">echo</hi> to that prophecy, and shows her to be no less filled with the Holy Ghost than Elisabeth was. We may suppose the blessed virgin to come in, very much <hi type="italic">fatigued</hi> with her journey; yet she forgets that, and is inspired with new life, and vigour, and joy, upon the confirmation she here meets with of her faith; and since, by the sudden inspiration and transport, she finds that this was designed to be her errand hither, weary as she is, like Abraham's servant, she would <hi type="italic">neither eat nor drink till she had told her errand.</hi> <div eID="gen25171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25172" type="x-p"/> 1. Here are the expressions of joy and praise, and God alone the object of the praise and centre of the joy. Some compare this song with that which her name-sake Miriam, the sister of Moses, sung, upon the triumphant departure of Israel out of Egypt, and their triumphant passage through the Red Sea; others think it better compared with the song of Hannah, upon the birth of Samuel, which, like this, passes from a family mercy to a public and general one. <hi type="italic">This</hi> begins, like <hi type="italic">that, My heart rejoiceth in the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1 Sam. ii. 1</reference>. Observe how Mary here speaks of God. <div eID="gen25172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25173" type="x-p"/> (1.) With great reverence of him, as <hi type="italic">the Lord:</hi> "<hi type="italic">My soul doth magnify the Lord;</hi> I never saw him so <hi type="italic">great</hi> as now I find him so <hi type="italic">good.</hi>" Note, Those, and those only, are <hi type="italic">advanced</hi> in mercy, who are thereby brought to think the more <hi type="italic">highly</hi> and <hi type="italic">honourably</hi> of God; whereas there are those whose prosperity and preferment make them say, <hi type="italic">What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?</hi> The more honour God has any way put upon us, the more honour we must study to give to him; and <hi type="italic">then</hi> only are we accepted in magnifying the Lord, when our <hi type="italic">souls</hi> magnify him, and <hi type="italic">all that is within us.</hi> Praising work must be soul work. <div eID="gen25173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25174" type="x-p"/> (2.) With great complacency in him as <hi type="italic">her Saviour: My spirit rejoiceth in God my Saviour.</hi> This seems to have reference to the Messiah, whom she was to be the mother of. She calls him <hi type="italic">God her Saviour;</hi> for the angel had told her that he should be the <hi type="italic">Son of the Highest,</hi> and that his name should be <hi type="italic">Jesus, a Saviour;</hi> this she fastened upon, with application to herself: <hi type="italic">He is God my Saviour.</hi> Even the mother of our Lord had need of an interest in him as her Saviour, and would have been undone without it: and she glories more in that happiness which she had in common with all believers than in being his mother, which was an honour peculiar to herself, and this agrees with the preference Christ have to obedient believers above his mother and brethren; see <reference osisRef="Matt.12.50">Matt. xii. 50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.27-Luke.11.28">Luke xi. 27, 28</reference>. Note, Those that have Christ for their God and Saviour have a great deal of reason to rejoice, to <hi type="italic">rejoice in spirit,</hi> that is rejoicing as Christ did (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">Luke x. 21</reference>), with spiritual joy. <div eID="gen25174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25175" type="x-p"/> 2. Here are just causes assigned for this joy and praise. <div eID="gen25175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25176" type="x-p"/> (1.) Upon <hi type="italic">her own</hi> account, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.48-Luke.1.49">v. 48, 49</reference>. [1.] Her <hi type="italic">spirit rejoiced in the Lord,</hi> because of the <hi type="italic">kind</hi> things he had done for her: his <hi type="italic">condescension</hi> and <hi type="italic">compassion</hi> to her. <hi type="italic">He has regarded the low estate of his handmaiden;</hi> that is, he has <hi type="italic">looked</hi> upon her <hi type="italic">with pity,</hi> for so the word is commonly used. "He has chosen me to this honour, notwithstanding my great meanness, poverty, and obscurity." Nay, the expression seems to intimate, not only (to allude to that of Gideon, <reference osisRef="Judg.6.15">Judg. vi. 15</reference>) that her <hi type="italic">family</hi> was poor in Judah, but that she was the <hi type="italic">least in her father's house,</hi> as if she were under some particular contempt and disgraced among her relations, was unjustly neglected, and the outcast of the family, and God put this honour upon her, to balance abundantly the contempt. I the rather suggest this, for we find something toward such honour as this put upon others, on the like consideration. Because God saw that Leah <hi type="italic">was hated,</hi> he <hi type="italic">opened her womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.29.31">Gen. xxix. 31</reference>. Because Hannah was provoked, and made to fret, and insulted over, by Peninnah, therefore God gave her a son, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.19">1 Sam. i. 19</reference>. Whom men wrongfully depress and despise God doth sometimes, in compassion to them, especially if they have borne it patiently, prefer and advance; see <reference osisRef="Judg.11.7">Judg. xi. 7</reference>. So in Mary's case. And, if God <hi type="italic">regards her low estate,</hi> he not only thereby gives a specimen of his favour to the whole race of mankind, whom he <hi type="italic">remembers in their low estate,</hi> as the psalmist speaks (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.23">Ps. cxxxvi. 23</reference>), but secures a lasting honour to her (for such the honour is that God bestows, honour that fades not away): "<hi type="italic">From henceforth all generations shall call me blessed,</hi> shall think me a happy woman and highly advanced." All that embrace Christ and his gospel will say, <hi type="italic">Blessed was the womb that bore him and the paps which he sucked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.27">Luke xi. 27</reference>. Elizabeth had once and again called her <hi type="italic">blessed:</hi> "But that is not all," saith she, "all generations of Gentiles as well as Jews shall call me so." [2.] Her <hi type="italic">soul magnifies</hi> the Lord, because of the <hi type="italic">wonderful</hi> things he had done for her (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that is mighty has done to me great things.</hi> A <hi type="italic">great</hi> thing indeed, that a <hi type="italic">virgin</hi> should <hi type="italic">conceive.</hi> A <hi type="italic">great</hi> thing indeed, that Messiah, who had been so long promised to the church, and so long expected by the church, should now at length be born. It is the <hi type="italic">power of the Highest</hi> that appears in this. She adds, <hi type="italic">and holy is his name;</hi> for so Hannah saith her song, <hi type="italic">There is none holy as the Lord,</hi> which she explains in the next words, <hi type="italic">for there is none beside thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.2">1 Sam. ii. 2</reference>. God is a Being <hi type="italic">by himself,</hi> and he manifests himself to be so, especially in the work of our redemption. He that is <hi type="italic">mighty,</hi> even he <hi type="italic">whose name is holy,</hi> has <hi type="italic">done to me great things.</hi> Glorious things may be expected from him that is both <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> and <hi type="italic">holy;</hi> who <hi type="italic">can do every thing,</hi> and <hi type="italic">will</hi> do every thing <hi type="italic">well</hi> and <hi type="italic">for the best.</hi> <div eID="gen25176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25177" type="x-p"/> (2.) Upon the account of <hi type="italic">others.</hi> The virgin Mary, as the mother of the Messiah, is become a kind of public person, wears a public character, and is therefore immediately endued with another spirit, a more public spirit than before she had, and therefore <hi type="italic">looks abroad,</hi> looks <hi type="italic">about her,</hi> looks <hi type="italic">before her,</hi> and takes notice of God's various dealings with the children of men (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.50">v. 50</reference>, &c.), as Hannah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1 Sam. ii. 3</reference>, &c.). In this she has especially an eye to the coming of the Redeemer and God's manifesting himself therein. <div eID="gen25177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25178" type="x-p"/> [1.] It is a certain truth that God <hi type="italic">has mercy in store,</hi> mercy in reserve, <hi type="italic">for all that have a reverence for his majesty,</hi> and a due regard to his sovereignty and authority. But never did this appear so as in sending his Son into the world to save us (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.50">v. 50</reference>): <hi type="italic">His mercy is on them that fear him;</hi> it has always been so; he has ever looked upon <hi type="italic">them</hi> with an eye of <hi type="italic">peculiar favour</hi> who have looked up to him with and eye of <hi type="italic">filial fear.</hi> But he hath manifested this <hi type="italic">mercy,</hi> so as never before, in sending his Son to bring in an everlasting righteousness, and work out an everlasting salvation, for them that fear him, and this <hi type="italic">from generation to generation;</hi> for there are gospel privileges transmitted by entail, and intended for perpetuity. Those that <hi type="italic">fear God,</hi> as their Creator and Judge, are encouraged to hope for <hi type="italic">mercy in him,</hi> through their Mediator and Advocate; and in him <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> is settled upon all that <hi type="italic">fear God,</hi> pardoning mercy, healing mercy, accepting mercy, crowning mercy, <hi type="italic">from generation to generation,</hi> while the world stands. In Christ he <hi type="italic">keepeth mercy for thousands.</hi> <div eID="gen25178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25179" type="x-p"/> [2.] It has been a common observation that God in his providence puts <hi type="italic">contempt</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">haughty</hi> and <hi type="italic">honour</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">humble;</hi> and this he has done remarkably in the whole economy of the work of man's redemption. As God had, with his <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> to her, shown himself <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> also (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.48-Luke.1.49">v. 48, 49</reference>), so he had, with his <hi type="italic">mercy on them that fear him, shown strength</hi> likewise <hi type="italic">with his arm.</hi> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In the course of his providence, it is his usual method to cross <hi type="italic">the expectations of men,</hi> and proceed quite otherwise than they promise themselves. <hi type="italic">Proud men</hi> expect to carry all before them, to have their way and their will; but he <hi type="italic">scatters them in the imagination of their hearts,</hi> breaks their measures, blasts their projects, nay, and brings them low, and brings them down, by those very counsels with which they thought to advance and establish themselves. The <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> think to secure themselves by might <hi type="italic">in their seats,</hi> but he <hi type="italic">puts them down,</hi> and overturns their seats; while, on the other hand, those of <hi type="italic">low degree,</hi> who despaired of ever advancing themselves, and thought of no other than of being <hi type="italic">ever low,</hi> are wonderfully <hi type="italic">exalted.</hi> This observation concerning <hi type="italic">honour</hi> holds likewise concerning <hi type="italic">riches;</hi> many who were so poor that they had not bread for themselves and their families, by some surprising turn of Providence in favour of them, come to be <hi type="italic">filled with good things;</hi> while, on the other hand, those who were rich, and thought no other than that to-morrow should be as this day, that their mountain stood strong and should never be moved, are strangely impoverished, and <hi type="italic">sent away empty.</hi> Now this is the same observation that Hannah had made, and enlarged upon, in her song, with application to the case of herself and her adversary (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.4-1Sam.2.7">1 Sam. ii. 4-7</reference>), which very much illustrates this here. And compare also <reference osisRef="Ps.107.33-Ps.107.41">Ps. cvii. 33-41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.113.7-Ps.113.9">cxiii. 7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">and Eccl. ix. 11</reference>. God takes a pleasure in <hi type="italic">disappointing</hi> their expectations who promise themselves <hi type="italic">great things</hi> in the world, and in <hi type="italic">out-doing</hi> the expectations of those who promise themselves but <hi type="italic">a little;</hi> as a <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> God, it is his glory to <hi type="italic">abase</hi> those who <hi type="italic">exalt</hi> themselves, and strike terror on the secure; and, as a <hi type="italic">good</hi> God, it is his glory to exalt those who humble themselves, and to speak comfort to those who fear before him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> This doth especially appear in the methods of gospel grace. <div eID="gen25179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25180" type="x-p"/> 1. In the <hi type="italic">spiritual honours</hi> it dispenses. When the proud Pharisees were rejected, and Publicans and sinners went <hi type="italic">into the kingdom of heaven</hi> before them,—when the Jews, who <hi type="italic">followed after the law of righteousness,</hi> did not attain it, and the Gentiles, who never thought of it, attained to righteousness (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.30-Rom.9.31">Rom. ix. 30, 31</reference>),—when God chose not the <hi type="italic">wise men after the flesh,</hi> not the <hi type="italic">mighty,</hi> or the <hi type="italic">noble,</hi> to preach the gospel, and plant Christianity in the world, but the <hi type="italic">foolish</hi> and <hi type="italic">weak</hi> things of the world, and things that were despised (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26-1Cor.1.27">1 Cor. i. 26, 27</reference>)—then he <hi type="italic">scattered the proud,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put down the mighty,</hi> but <hi type="italic">exalted them of low degree.</hi> When the tyranny of the chief priests and elders were brought down, who had long <hi type="italic">lorded it over God's heritage,</hi> and hoped <hi type="italic">always</hi> to do so, and Christ's disciples, a company of poor despised fishermen, by the power they were clothed with, were made to <hi type="italic">sit on thrones,</hi> judging the twelve tribes of Israel,—when the power of the four monarchies was broken, and the kingdom of the Messiah, that <hi type="italic">stone cut out of the mountain without hands,</hi> is made to <hi type="italic">fill the earth,</hi>—then are the <hi type="italic">proud scattered,</hi> and those of low degree <hi type="italic">exalted.</hi> <div eID="gen25180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25181" type="x-p"/> 2. In the <hi type="italic">spiritual riches</hi> it dispenses, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">v. 53</reference>. (1.) Those who see their need of Christ, and are importunately desirous of righteousness and life in him, he <hi type="italic">fills</hi> with <hi type="italic">good things,</hi> with the <hi type="italic">best things;</hi> he gives liberally to them, and they are <hi type="italic">abundantly satisfied</hi> with the blessings he gives. Those who are weary and heavy-laden shall find rest with Christ, and those who thirst are called to <hi type="italic">come to him and drink;</hi> for they only know how to value his gifts. <hi type="italic">To the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet,</hi> manna is angels' food; and to the <hi type="italic">thirsty</hi> fair water is <hi type="italic">honey out of the rock.</hi> (2.) Those who are rich, who are not <hi type="italic">hungry,</hi> who, like Laodicea, think they have <hi type="italic">need of nothing,</hi> are full of themselves and their own righteousness, and think they have a sufficiency in themselves, those he <hi type="italic">sends away</hi> from his door, they are not welcome to him, he sends them <hi type="italic">empty</hi> away, they come <hi type="italic">full of self,</hi> and are sent away <hi type="italic">empty of Christ.</hi> He sends them to the <hi type="italic">gods whom they served,</hi> to their own righteousness and strength which they trusted to. <div eID="gen25181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25182" type="x-p"/> [3.] It was always expected that the Messiah should be, in a special manner, the strength and glory of his people Israel, and so he is in a peculiar manner (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.54">v. 54</reference>): <hi type="italic">He hath helped his servant Israel,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">antelabeto</hi></hi>. He hath taken them by the hand, and <hi type="italic">helped them up</hi> that were fallen and could not help themselves. Those that were sunk under the burdens of a broken covenant of innocency are <hi type="italic">helped up</hi> by the blessings of a renewed covenant of grace. The sending of the Messiah, on whom <hi type="italic">help</hi> was <hi type="italic">laid</hi> for poor sinners, was the greatest kindness that could be done, the greatest help that could be provided for his people Israel, and that which magnifies it is, <div eID="gen25182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25183" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That it is <hi type="italic">in remembrance of his mercy,</hi> the mercifulness of his nature, the mercy he has in store for <hi type="italic">his servant Israel.</hi> While this blessing was deferred, his people, who waited for it, were often ready to ask, <hi type="italic">Has God forgotten to be gracious?</hi> But now he made it appear that he had not forgotten, but <hi type="italic">remembered, his mercy.</hi> He remembered his former mercy, and repeated that to them in <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> blessings which he had done formerly to them in <hi type="italic">temporal</hi> favours. <hi type="italic">He remembered the days of old. Where is he that brought them up out of the sea,</hi> out of Egypt? <reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Isa. lxiii. 11</reference>. He will do the like again, which that was a type of. <div eID="gen25183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25184" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That it is <hi type="italic">in performance of his promise.</hi> It is a mercy not only designed, but declared (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.55">v. 55</reference>); it was <hi type="italic">what he spoke to our fathers,</hi> that the Seed of the woman should break the head of the serpent; that God should dwell in the tents of Shem; and particularly to Abraham, that <hi type="italic">in his seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed,</hi> with the best of blessings, with the blessings that are <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> and to the seed that shall be for ever; that is, his <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> seed, for his carnal seed were <hi type="italic">cut off</hi> a little after this. Note, What God has spoken he will perform; what he hath spoken to the fathers will be performed to their seed; to their seed's seed, in blessings that shall last for ever. <div eID="gen25184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25185" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Mary's return to Nazareth (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.56">v. 56</reference>), after she had continued with Elisabeth about <hi type="italic">three months,</hi> so long as to be fully satisfied concerning herself that she was <hi type="italic">with child,</hi> and to be confirmed therein by her cousin Elisabeth. Some think, though her return is here mentioned before Elisabeth's being delivered, because the evangelist would finish this passage concerning Mary before he proceeded with the story of Elisabeth, yet that Mary staid till her cousin was (as we say) <hi type="italic">down and up again;</hi> that she might attend on her, and be with her in her lying-in, and have her own faith confirmed by the full accomplishment of the promise of God concerning Elisabeth. But most bind themselves to the order of the story as it lies, and think she returned again when Elisabeth was near her time; because she still affected retirement, and therefore would not be there when the birth of this child of promise would draw a great deal of company to the house. Those in whose hearts Christ is formed take more delight than they used to do in <hi type="italic">sitting alone</hi> and <hi type="italic">keeping silence.</hi>
entries.3d11fa4b3bc8f5b7aaf39df67101459fda51ac94: <div eID="gen25185" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Birth of John the Baptist.</title> <div sID="gen25186" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">57</hi> Now Elisabeth's full time came that she should be delivered; and she brought forth a son. <hi type="super">58</hi> And her neighbours and her cousins heard how the Lord had showed great mercy upon her; and they rejoiced with her. <hi type="super">59</hi> And it came to pass, that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child; and they called him Zacharias, after the name of his father. <hi type="super">60</hi> And his mother answered and said, Not <hi type="italic">so;</hi> but he shall be called <reference osisRef="John.61">John. 61</reference> And they said unto her, There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name. <hi type="super">62</hi> And they made signs to his father, how he would have him called. <hi type="super">63</hi> And he asked for a writing table, and wrote, saying, His name is John. And they marvelled all. <hi type="super">64</hi> And his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue <hi type="italic">loosed,</hi> and he spake, and praised God. <hi type="super">65</hi> And fear came on all that dwelt round about them: and all these sayings were noised abroad throughout all the hill country of Judæa. <hi type="super">66</hi> And all they that heard <hi type="italic">them</hi> laid <hi type="italic">them</hi> up in their hearts, saying, What manner of child shall this be! And the hand of the Lord was with him. <div eID="gen25186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25187" type="x-p"/> In these verses, we have, <div eID="gen25187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25188" type="x-p"/> I. The birth of John Baptist, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.57">v. 57</reference>. Though he was conceived in the womb by miracle, he continued in the womb according to the ordinary course of nature (so did our Saviour): <hi type="italic">Elisabeth's full time came, that she should be delivered,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">she brought forth a son.</hi> Promised mercies are to be expected when the <hi type="italic">full time</hi> for them is come, and not before. <div eID="gen25188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25189" type="x-p"/> II. The great joy that was among all the relations of the family, upon this extraordinary occasion (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.58">v. 58</reference>): <hi type="italic">Her neighbours and her cousins heard of it;</hi> for it would be in every body's mouth, as next to miraculous. Dr. Lightfoot observes that Hebron was inhabited by priests of the family of Aaron, and that those were the cousins here spoken of; but the fields and villages about, by the children of Judah, and that those were the <hi type="italic">neighbours.</hi> Now these here discovered, 1. A <hi type="italic">pious</hi> regard to God. They acknowledged that <hi type="italic">the Lord had magnified his mercy to her,</hi> so the word is. It was a mercy to have her reproach taken away, a mercy to have her family built up, and the more being a family of <hi type="italic">priests,</hi> devoted to God, and employed for him. Many things concurred to make the mercy <hi type="italic">great</hi>—that she had been long barren, was now old, but especially that the child should be <hi type="italic">great in the sight of the Lord.</hi> 2. A <hi type="italic">friendly</hi> regard to Elisabeth. When she rejoiced, they <hi type="italic">rejoiced with her.</hi> We ought to take <hi type="italic">pleasure</hi> in the prosperity of our neighbours and friends, and to be thankful to God for <hi type="italic">their</hi> comforts as for our own. <div eID="gen25189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25190" type="x-p"/> III. The dispute that was among them concerning the naming him (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.59">v. 59</reference>): <hi type="italic">On the eighth day,</hi> as God has appointed, they <hi type="italic">came together,</hi> to <hi type="italic">circumcise the child;</hi> it was here, in Hebron, that <hi type="italic">circumcision</hi> was first instituted; and Isaac, who, like John Baptist, was born <hi type="italic">by promise,</hi> was one of the first that was submitted to it, at least the chief eyed in the institution of it. They that rejoiced in the birth of the child came together to the circumcising of him. Note, The greatest comfort we can take in our children is in <hi type="italic">giving them up to God,</hi> and recognizing their covenant-relation to him. The baptism of our children should be more our joy than their birth. <div eID="gen25190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25191" type="x-p"/> Now it was the custom, when they circumcised their children, to <hi type="italic">name them,</hi> because, when <hi type="italic">Abram</hi> was circumcised God gave him a new name, and called him <hi type="italic">Abraham;</hi> and it is not unfit that they should be left <hi type="italic">nameless</hi> till they are by name <hi type="italic">given up to God.</hi> Now, <div eID="gen25191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25192" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Some</hi> proposed that he should be called by his father's name, <hi type="italic">Zacharias.</hi> We have not any instance in scripture that the child should bear the father's name; but perhaps it was of late come into use among the Jews, at it is with us, and they intended hereby to do honour to the father, who was not likely to have another child. <div eID="gen25192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25193" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">mother</hi> opposed it, and would have called him <hi type="italic">John;</hi> having learned, either by inspiration of the Holy Ghost (as is most probable), or by information in writing from her husband, that God appointed this to be his name (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.60">v. 60</reference>); He shall be called <hi type="italic">Johanan—Gracious,</hi> because he shall introduce the gospel of Christ, wherein God's grace shines more brightly than ever. <div eID="gen25193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25194" type="x-p"/> 3. The <hi type="italic">relations</hi> objected against that (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.61">v. 61</reference>): "<hi type="italic">There is none of thy kindred,</hi> none of the relations of thy family, <hi type="italic">that is called by that name;</hi> and therefore, if he may not have his father's name, yet let him have the name of some of his kindred, who will take it as a piece of respect to have such a <hi type="italic">child of wonders</hi> as this named from them." Note, As those that <hi type="italic">have friends</hi> must <hi type="italic">show themselves friendly,</hi> so those that have relations must be <hi type="italic">obliging</hi> to them in all the usual regards that are paid to <hi type="italic">kindred.</hi> <div eID="gen25194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25195" type="x-p"/> 4. They appealed to the <hi type="italic">father,</hi> and would try if they could possibly get to know his mind; for it was his office to <hi type="italic">name the child,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.62">v. 62</reference>. They <hi type="italic">made signs</hi> to him, by which it appears that he was <hi type="italic">deaf</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">dumb;</hi> nay, it should seem, <hi type="italic">mindless</hi> of any thing, else one would think they should at first have desired him to write down his child's name, if he had ever communicated any thing by writing since he was <hi type="italic">struck.</hi> However, they would carry the matter as far as they could, and therefore gave him to understand what the dispute was which he only could determine; whereupon he made signs to them to give him a <hi type="italic">table-book,</hi> such as they then used, and with the pencil he wrote these words, <hi type="italic">His name is John,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.63">v. 63</reference>. Note, "It shall be so," or, "I would have it so," but "It is so." The matter is determined already; the <hi type="italic">angel</hi> had given him that name. Observe, When Zacharias could not <hi type="italic">speak,</hi> he <hi type="italic">wrote.</hi> When ministers have their mouths stopped, that they cannot preach, yet they may be doing good as long as they have not their hands tied, that they cannot write. Many of the martyrs in prison wrote letters to their friends, which were of great use; blessed Paul himself did so. Zacharias's pitching upon the same name that Elisabeth had chosen was a great surprise to the company: <hi type="italic">They marvelled all;</hi> for they knew not that, though by reason of his deafness and dumbness they could not <hi type="italic">converse together,</hi> yet they were both guided by <hi type="italic">one and the same Spirit:</hi> or perhaps they <hi type="italic">marvelled</hi> that he wrote so distinctly and intelligently, which (the stroke he was under being somewhat like that of a palsy) he had not done before. <div eID="gen25195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25196" type="x-p"/> 5. He thereupon recovered the use of his speech (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.64">v. 64</reference>): <hi type="italic">His mouth was opened immediately.</hi> The time prefixed for his being silenced was <hi type="italic">till the day that these blessed things shall be fulfilled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.20">v. 20</reference>); not <hi type="italic">all the things</hi> going before concerning John's ministry, but those which relate to his birth and name (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.13">v. 13</reference>). That time was now expired, whereupon the restraint was taken off, and God gave him the <hi type="italic">opening of the mouth again,</hi> as he did to Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.27">ch. iii. 27</reference>. Dr. Lightfoot compares this case of Zacharias with that of Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.4.24-Exod.4.26">Exod. iv. 24-26</reference>. Moses, for distrust, is in danger of his life, as Zacharias, for the same fault, is <hi type="italic">struck dumb;</hi> but, upon the circumcision of his child, and recovery of his faith, there, as here, the danger is removed. Infidelity closed his mouth, and now believing opens it again; <hi type="italic">he believes, therefore he speaks.</hi> David lay under guilt from the conception of his child till a few days after its birth; then <hi type="italic">the Lord takes away his sin:</hi> upon his repentance, he shall not die. So here he shall be no longer dumb; <hi type="italic">his mouth was opened, and he spoke, and praised God.</hi> Note, When God opens our lips, our mouths must <hi type="italic">show forth his praise.</hi> As good be without our speech as not use it in <hi type="italic">praising God;</hi> for then our tongue is most <hi type="italic">our glory</hi> when it is employed for <hi type="italic">God's glory.</hi> <div eID="gen25196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25197" type="x-p"/> 6. These things were told all the country over, to the great amazement of all that heard them, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.65-Luke.1.66">v. 65, 66</reference>. The sentiments of the people are not to be slighted, but taken notice of. We are here told, (1.) That <hi type="italic">these sayings were discoursed of,</hi> and were the common talk all about the <hi type="italic">hill-country of Judea.</hi> It is a pity but a narrative of them had been drawn up, and published in the world, immediately. (2.) That most people who heard of these things were put into consternation by them: <hi type="italic">Fear came on all them that dwell round about</hi> there. If we have not a <hi type="italic">good hope,</hi> as we ought to have, built upon the gospel, we may expect that the tidings of it will fill us with <hi type="italic">fear.</hi> They believed and trembled, whereas they should have believed and triumphed. (3.) It raised the expectations of people concerning this child, and obliged them to have their eye upon him, to see what he would come to. They <hi type="italic">laid up these</hi> presages <hi type="italic">in their hearts,</hi> treasured them up in mind and memory, as foreseeing they should hereafter have occasion to <hi type="italic">recollect</hi> them. Note, What we hear, that may be of use to us, we should <hi type="italic">treasure</hi> up, that we may be able to bring forth, for the benefit of others, things new and old, and, when things come to perfection, may be able to look back upon the presages thereof, and to say, "It was what we might expect." They said <hi type="italic">within</hi> themselves, and said <hi type="italic">among</hi> themselves, "<hi type="italic">What manner of child shall this be?</hi> What will be the fruit when these are the buds, or rather when the <hi type="italic">root</hi> is out of such a <hi type="italic">dry ground?</hi>" Note, When children are born into the world, it is very uncertain what they will prove; yet sometimes there have been early indications of something great, as in the birth of Moses, Samson, Samuel, and here of John. And we have reason to think that there were some of those living at the time when John began his public ministry who could, and did, remember these things, and relate them to others, which contributed as much as any thing to the great flocking there was after him. <div eID="gen25197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25198" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> It is said, <hi type="italic">The hand of the Lord was with him;</hi> that is, he was taken under the special protection of the Almighty, from his birth, as one designed for something great and considerable, and there were many instances of it. It appeared likewise that the Spirit was at work upon his soul very early. As soon as he began to speak or go, you might perceive something in him very extraordinary. Note, God has ways of operating upon children in their infancy, which we cannot account for. God never made a soul but he knew how to sanctify it.
entries.9c631e7d3c08fa79fd856d64827f1c556d397052: <div eID="gen25198" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Song of Zacharias.</title> <div sID="gen25199" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">67</hi> And his father Zacharias was filled with the Holy Ghost, and prophesied, saying, <hi type="super">68</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people, 69 And hath raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David; <hi type="super">70</hi> As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: <hi type="super">71</hi> That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us; <hi type="super">72</hi> To perform the mercy <hi type="italic">promised</hi> to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant; <hi type="super">73</hi> The oath which he sware to our father Abraham, <hi type="super">74</hi> That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear, <hi type="super">75</hi> In holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. <hi type="super">76</hi> And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways; <hi type="super">77</hi> To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins, <hi type="super">78</hi> Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, <hi type="super">79</hi> To give light to them that sit in darkness and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace. <hi type="super">80</hi> And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his showing unto Israel. <div eID="gen25199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25200" type="x-p"/> We have here the song wherewith Zacharias <hi type="italic">praised God</hi> when his <hi type="italic">mouth</hi> was <hi type="italic">opened;</hi> in it he is said to <hi type="italic">prophesy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.67">v. 67</reference>), and so he did in the strictest sense of <hi type="italic">prophesying;</hi> for he foretold things to come concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, to which all the prophets bear witness. Observe, <div eID="gen25200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25201" type="x-p"/> I. How he was qualified for this: <hi type="italic">He was filled with the Holy Ghost,</hi> was endued with more than ordinary measures and degrees of it, for this purpose; he was divinely inspired. God not only <hi type="italic">forgave</hi> him his unbelief and distrust (which was signified by discharging him from the punishment of it), but, as a <hi type="italic">specimen</hi> of the <hi type="italic">abounding</hi> of grace towards believers, he <hi type="italic">filled him</hi> with the <hi type="italic">Holy Ghost,</hi> and put this honour upon him, to employ him for his honour. <div eID="gen25201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25202" type="x-p"/> II. What the matter of his song was. Here is nothing said of the private concerns of his own family, the rolling away of the reproach from it and putting of a reputation upon it, by the birth of this child, though, no doubt, he found a time to give thanks to God for this, with his family; but in this song he is wholly taken up with the kingdom of the Messiah, and the public blessings to be introduced by it. He could have little pleasure in this <hi type="italic">fruitfulness</hi> of his <hi type="italic">vine,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">hopefulness</hi> of his <hi type="italic">olive-plant,</hi> if herein he had not foreseen the <hi type="italic">good of Jerusalem, peace upon Israel,</hi> and <hi type="italic">blessings</hi> on both <hi type="italic">out of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.128.3">Ps. cxxviii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.5">5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.6">6</reference>. The Old-Testament prophesies are often expressed in <hi type="italic">praises</hi> and <hi type="italic">new songs,</hi> so is the beginning of New-Testament prophecy: <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord God of Israel. The God of the whole earth shall he be called;</hi> yet Zacharias, speaking of the work of redemption, called him the <hi type="italic">Lord God of Israel,</hi> because to Israel the prophecies, promises, and types, of the redemption had hitherto been given, and to them the first proffers and proposals of it were now to be made. Israel, as a chosen people, was a type of the <hi type="italic">elect of God</hi> out of all nations, whom God had a particular eye to, in sending the Saviour; and therefore he is therein called the <hi type="italic">Lord God of Israel.</hi> <div eID="gen25202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25203" type="x-p"/> Now Zacharias here blesses God, <div eID="gen25203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25204" type="x-p"/> 1. For the work of <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> that was to be wrought out by the Messiah himself, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.68-Luke.1.75">v. 68-75</reference>. This it is that <hi type="italic">fills him,</hi> when he is <hi type="italic">filled with the Holy Ghost,</hi> and it is that which all who have the <hi type="italic">Spirit of Christ</hi> are <hi type="italic">full of.</hi> <div eID="gen25204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25205" type="x-p"/> (1.) In sending the Messiah, God has <hi type="italic">made a gracious visit</hi> to his people, whom for many ages he had seemed to neglect, and to be estranged from; he hath <hi type="italic">visited them</hi> as a friend, to take cognizance of their case. God is said to have <hi type="italic">visited</hi> his people in bondage when he <hi type="italic">delivered</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.16">Exod. iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.4.31">iv. 31</reference>), to have <hi type="italic">visited</hi> his people in famine when he <hi type="italic">gave them bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.6">Ruth i. 6</reference>. He had often sent to them by his prophets, and had still kept up a correspondence with them; but now he himself made them a <hi type="italic">visit.</hi> <div eID="gen25205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25206" type="x-p"/> (2.) He has <hi type="italic">wrought out redemption</hi> for them: <hi type="italic">He has redeemed his people.</hi> This was the errand on which Christ <hi type="italic">came into the world,</hi> to redeem those that were sold <hi type="italic">for</hi> sin, and sold <hi type="italic">under</hi> sin; even God's own people, his Israel, his son, his <hi type="italic">first-born,</hi> his <hi type="italic">free-born,</hi> need to be <hi type="italic">redeemed,</hi> and are undone if they be not. Christ redeems them by <hi type="italic">price</hi> out of the hands of God's justice, and redeems them by <hi type="italic">power</hi> out of the hands of Satan's tyranny, as Israel out of Egypt. <div eID="gen25206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25207" type="x-p"/> (3.) He has fulfilled the <hi type="italic">covenant of royalty</hi> made with the most famous <hi type="italic">Old-Testament prince,</hi> that is, David. Glorious things had been said of his family, that on him, as a <hi type="italic">mighty one, help</hi> should be <hi type="italic">laid,</hi> that <hi type="italic">his horn should be exalted,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">seed</hi> perpetuated, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.19-Ps.89.20">Ps. lxxxix. 19, 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.24">24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">29</reference>. But that family had been long in a manner <hi type="italic">cast off</hi> and <hi type="italic">abhorred,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.38">Ps. lxxxix. 38</reference>. Now here it is glorified in, that, according to the promise, the <hi type="italic">horn</hi> of David should again be <hi type="italic">made to bud;</hi> for, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Ps. cxxxii. 17</reference>, he <hi type="italic">hath raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">v. 69</reference>), there, where it was promised and expected to arise. David is called God's <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> not only as a good man, but as a king that <hi type="italic">ruled for God;</hi> and he was an instrument of the <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> of Israel, by being employed in the <hi type="italic">government</hi> of Israel; so Christ is the <hi type="italic">author of eternal redemption to those</hi> only <hi type="italic">that obey him.</hi> There is in Christ, and in him only, <hi type="italic">salvation for us,</hi> and it is a <hi type="italic">horn of salvation;</hi> for, [1.] It is an <hi type="italic">honourable</hi> salvation. It is <hi type="italic">raised up</hi> above all other salvations, none of which are to be compared with it: in it the glory both of the Redeemer and of the redeemed are advanced, and their <hi type="italic">horn exalted with honour.</hi> [2.] It is a <hi type="italic">plentiful salvation.</hi> It is a <hi type="italic">cornucopia—a horn of plenty,</hi> a <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> in which we are blessed with <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> blessings, in <hi type="italic">heavenly things,</hi> abundantly. [3.] It is a <hi type="italic">powerful salvation:</hi> the strength of the beast is in his <hi type="italic">horn.</hi> He has raised up such a salvation as shall <hi type="italic">pull down</hi> our spiritual enemies, and <hi type="italic">protect</hi> us from them. In the <hi type="italic">chariots</hi> of this <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> the Redeemer shall go forth, and go on, <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer.</hi> <div eID="gen25207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25208" type="x-p"/> (4.) He has fulfilled all the precious promises made to the church by the most famous <hi type="italic">Old-Testament prophets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.70">v. 70</reference>): <hi type="italic">As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets.</hi> His doctrine of salvation by the Messiah is confirmed by an appeal to the prophets, and the greatness and importance of that salvation thereby evidenced and magnified; it is the same that they spoke of, which therefore ought to be expected and welcomed; it is what they <hi type="italic">enquired and searched diligently after</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10-1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 10, 11</reference>), which therefore ought not to be slighted or thought meanly of. God is now <hi type="italic">doing</hi> that which he has long ago <hi type="italic">spoken of;</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">be silent, O all flesh, before him,</hi> and attend to him. See, [1.] How <hi type="italic">sacred</hi> the prophecies of this salvation were. The prophets who delivered them were <hi type="italic">holy prophets,</hi> who durst not deceive and who aimed at promoting holiness among men; and it was the <hi type="italic">holy God</hi> himself that <hi type="italic">spoke by</hi> them. [2.] How <hi type="italic">ancient</hi> they were: ever <hi type="italic">since the world began.</hi> God having promised, when the world began, that the <hi type="italic">Seed of the woman should break the serpent's head,</hi> that promise was echoed to when Adam called his wife's name <hi type="italic">Eve-Life,</hi> for the sake of that Seed of hers; when Eve called her first son <hi type="italic">Cain,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">I have gotten a man from the Lord,</hi> and another son, Seth, <hi type="italic">settled;</hi> when Noah was called <hi type="italic">rest,</hi> and foretold that God should dwell in the tents of Shem. And it was not long after the new world began in Noah that the promise was made to Abraham that in his Seed the <hi type="italic">nations of the earth</hi> should be <hi type="italic">blessed.</hi> [3.] What a wonderful <hi type="italic">harmony</hi> and <hi type="italic">concert</hi> we perceive among them. God spoke the same thing by them all, and therefore it is said to be <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dia stomatos</hi></hi>, not by the <hi type="italic">mouths,</hi> but by the <hi type="italic">mouth,</hi> of the prophets, for they all speak of Christ as it were with <hi type="italic">one mouth.</hi> <div eID="gen25208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25209" type="x-p"/> Now what is this <hi type="italic">salvation</hi> which was prophesied of? <div eID="gen25209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25210" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is a <hi type="italic">rescue</hi> from the malice of <hi type="italic">our enemies;</hi> it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">soterian ex echthron hemon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a salvation out of our enemies,</hi> from among them, and <hi type="italic">out of the power of them that hate us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.71">v. 71</reference>); it is a salvation from sin, and the dominion of Satan over us, both by corruptions within and temptations without. The carnal Jews expected to be delivered from under the Roman yoke, but intimation was betimes given that it should be a redemption of another nature. He shall <hi type="italic">save his people from their sins,</hi> that they may not have dominion over them, <reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Matt. i. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen25210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25211" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a <hi type="italic">restoration</hi> to the <hi type="italic">favour of God;</hi> it is to <hi type="italic">perform the mercy promised to our forefathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.72">v. 72</reference>. The Redeemer shall not only break the head of the serpent that was the author of our ruin, but he shall <hi type="italic">re-instate</hi> us in the <hi type="italic">mercy of God</hi> and <hi type="italic">re-establish</hi> us in <hi type="italic">his covenant;</hi> he shall bring us as it were into a paradise again, which was signified by the <hi type="italic">promises</hi> made to the patriarchs, and the <hi type="italic">holy covenant</hi> made with them, <hi type="italic">the oath which he sware to our father Abraham,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.73">v. 73</reference>. Observe, 1. That which was promised to the fathers, and is performed to us, is <hi type="italic">mercy,</hi> pure mercy; nothing in it is owing to our <hi type="italic">merit</hi> (we deserve wrath and the curse), but all to the <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> of God, which <hi type="italic">designed</hi> us grace and life: <hi type="italic">ex mero motu—of his own good pleasure,</hi> he loved us because he would love us. 2.
