God herein had an eye to <hi type="italic">his covenant,</hi> his <hi type="italic">holy</hi> covenant, that covenant with Abraham: <hi type="italic">I will be a God to thee and thy seed.</hi> This his seed had <hi type="italic">really forfeited</hi> by their transgressions; this he <hi type="italic">seemed to have forgotten</hi> in the calamities brought upon them; but he will now <hi type="italic">remember</hi> it, will make it appear that he remembers it, for upon that are grounded all his returns of mercy: <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev. xxvi. 42</reference>, <hi type="italic">Then will I remember my covenant.</hi> <div eID="gen25211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25212" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is a qualification for, and an encouragement to, the service of God. Thus was <hi type="italic">the oath he sware to our Father Abraham,</hi> That he would <hi type="italic">give us</hi> power and grace to <hi type="italic">serve him,</hi> in an acceptable manner to him and a comfortable manner to ourselves, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">v. 74, 75</reference>. Here seems to be an allusion to the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, which, God tells Moses, was in pursuance of the covenant he made with Abraham (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.6-Exod.3.8">Exod. iii. 6-8</reference>), and that this was the design of his bringing them out of Egypt, <hi type="italic">that they might serve God upon this mountain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.3.12">Exod. iii. 12</reference>. Note, The great design of gospel grace is not to discharge us from, but to engage us to, and encourage us in, the service of God. Under this notion Christianity was always to be looked upon, as intended to make us truly religious, to admit us into the service of God, to bind us to it, and to quicken us in it. We are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> delivered from the iron yoke of sin, that our necks may be put under the sweet and easy yoke of the Lord Jesus. <hi type="italic">The very bonds which he has loosed do bind us faster unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Ps. cxvi. 16</reference>. We are hereby enabled, 1. To serve God <hi type="italic">without fear</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aphobos</hi></hi>. We are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> put into a state of <hi type="italic">holy safety</hi> that we might serve God with a <hi type="italic">holy security</hi> and <hi type="italic">serenity of mind,</hi> as those that are <hi type="italic">quiet from the fears of evil.</hi> God must be served with a <hi type="italic">filial fear,</hi> a reverent obedient fear, an awakening quickening fear, but not with a <hi type="italic">slavish fear,</hi> like that of the slothful servant, who represented him to himself as a <hi type="italic">hard master,</hi> and unreasonable; not with that fear that has <hi type="italic">torment</hi> and <hi type="italic">amazement</hi> in it; not with the fear of a legal spirit; a <hi type="italic">spirit of bondage,</hi> but with the boldness of an evangelical spirit, <hi type="italic">a spirit of adoption.</hi> 2. To serve him in <hi type="italic">holiness and righteousness,</hi> which includes the whole duty of man towards God and our neighbour. It is both the intention and the direct tendency of the gospel to renew upon us that image of God in which man was at first made, which consisted <hi type="italic">in righteousness and true holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Ps. l. 14</reference>. 3. To serve him, <hi type="italic">before him,</hi> in the duties of his <hi type="italic">immediate</hi> worship, wherein we present ourselves <hi type="italic">before the Lord,</hi> to serve him as those that have an eye always upon him, and see his eye always upon us, upon our inward man, that is serving him <hi type="italic">before him.</hi> 4. To serve him <hi type="italic">all the days of our life.</hi> The design of the gospel is to engage us in constancy and perseverance in the service of God, by showing us how much depends upon our not drawing back, and by showing us how Christ <hi type="italic">loved us to the end,</hi> and thereby engaged us to <hi type="italic">love him to the end.</hi> <div eID="gen25212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25213" type="x-p"/> 2. He <hi type="italic">blessed God</hi> for the work of <hi type="italic">preparation</hi> for this salvation, which was to be done by John Baptist (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.76">v. 76</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou child,</hi> though now but a child of eight days' old, shalt be called <hi type="italic">the prophet of the Highest.</hi> Jesus Christ is <hi type="italic">the Highest,</hi> for he is <hi type="italic">God over all, blessed for evermore</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Rom. ix. 5</reference>), equal with the Father. John Baptist was <hi type="italic">his prophet,</hi> as Aaron was Moses's prophet (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.1">Exod. vii. 1</reference>); what he said was as his mouth, what he did was as his harbinger. Prophecy had now long ceased, but in John it <hi type="italic">revived,</hi> as it had done in Samuel, who was born of an aged mother, as John was, after a long cessation. John's business was, <div eID="gen25213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25214" type="x-p"/> (1.) To prepare people for the salvation, by preaching repentance and reformation as great gospel duties: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt go before the face of the Lord,</hi> and but a little before him, to <hi type="italic">prepare his ways,</hi> to call people to make room for him, and get ready for his entertainment. Let every thing that may obstruct his progress, or embarrass it, or hinder people from coming to him, be taken away: see <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3-Isa.40.4">Isa. xl. 3, 4</reference>. Let <hi type="italic">valleys be filled,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hills</hi> be brought <hi type="italic">low.</hi> <div eID="gen25214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25215" type="x-p"/> (2.) To give people a general idea of the salvation, that they might know, not only what to do, but what to expect; for the doctrine he preached was that the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven</hi> is at hand. There are two things in which you must know that this salvation consists:— <div eID="gen25215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25216" type="x-p"/> [1.] The <hi type="italic">forgiveness</hi> of what we have <hi type="italic">done amiss.</hi> It is salvation <hi type="italic">by the remission of sins,</hi> those sins which stand in the way of the salvation, and by which we are all become liable to ruin and condemnation, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.77">v. 77</reference>. John Baptist gave people to understand that, though their case was sad, by reason of sin, it was not desperate, for pardon might be obtained <hi type="italic">through the tender mercy of our God</hi> (the <hi type="italic">bowels of mercy,</hi> so the word is): there was nothing in us but a <hi type="italic">piteous case</hi> to recommend us to the divine compassion. <div eID="gen25216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25217" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">Direction</hi> to <hi type="italic">do better</hi> for the time to come. The gospel salvation not only encourages us to hope that the works of darkness shall be forgiven us, but sets up a clear and true light, by which we may order our steps aright. In it <hi type="italic">the day-spring hath visited us from on high</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.78">v. 78</reference>); and this also is owing to the <hi type="italic">tender mercy of our God.</hi> Christ is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anatole</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the morning Light,</hi> the <hi type="italic">rising Sun,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.2">Mal. iv. 2</reference>. The gospel brings <hi type="italic">light</hi> with it (<reference osisRef="John.3.19">John iii. 19</reference>), leaves us not to wander in the darkness of Pagan ignorance, or in the moonlight of the Old-Testament types or figures, but in it the day dawns; in John Baptist it began to break, but increased apace, and <hi type="italic">shone more and more to the perfect day.</hi> We have as much reason to welcome the gospel day who enjoy it as those have to welcome the morning who had long waited for it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The gospel is <hi type="italic">discovering;</hi> it shows us that which before we were utterly in the dark about (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.79">v. 79</reference>); it is to <hi type="italic">give light to them that sit in darkness,</hi> the <hi type="italic">light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ;</hi> the day-spring <hi type="italic">visited</hi> this dark world to <hi type="italic">lighten the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Acts xxvi. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is <hi type="italic">reviving;</hi> it brings light to them that sit <hi type="italic">in the shadow of death,</hi> as condemned prisoners in the dungeon, to bring them the tidings of a <hi type="italic">pardon,</hi> at least of a <hi type="italic">reprieve</hi> and opportunity of procuring a pardon; it proclaims the <hi type="italic">opening of the prison</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>), brings the <hi type="italic">light of life.</hi> How pleasant is that light! <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is <hi type="italic">directing;</hi> it is to <hi type="italic">guide our feet in the way of peace,</hi> into that way which will bring us to peace at last. It is not only a light <hi type="italic">to our eyes,</hi> but a light <hi type="italic">to our feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.105">Ps. cxix. 105</reference>); it guides us into the way of making our peace with God, of keeping up a comfortable communion; that <hi type="italic">way of peace</hi> which as sinners we have wandered from and <hi type="italic">have not known</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.17">Rom. iii. 17</reference>), nor could ever have known of ourselves. <div eID="gen25217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25218" type="x-p"/> In the <reference osisRef="Luke.1.80">last verse</reference>, we have short account of the younger years of John Baptist. Though he was the son of a priest, he did not, like Samuel, go up, when he was a child, to minister before the Lord; for he was to prepare the way for a better priesthood. But we are here told, <div eID="gen25218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25219" type="x-p"/> 1. Of his <hi type="italic">eminence</hi> as to the <hi type="italic">inward man:</hi> The <hi type="italic">child grew</hi> in the capacities of his mind, much more than other children; so that he <hi type="italic">waxed strong in the spirit;</hi> had a strong judgment and strong resolution. Reason and conscience (both which are the candle of the Lord) were so strong in him that he had the inferior faculties of appetite and passion in complete subjection betimes. By this it appeared that he was betimes <hi type="italic">filled with the Holy Ghost;</hi> for those that are strong in the Lord are <hi type="italic">strong in spirit.</hi> <div eID="gen25219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25220" type="x-p"/> 2. Of his <hi type="italic">obscurity</hi> as to the <hi type="italic">outward man:</hi> He <hi type="italic">was in the deserts;</hi> not that he lived a hermit; cut off from the society of men. No, we have reason to think that he went up to Jerusalem at the <hi type="italic">feasts,</hi> and frequented the synagogues on the sabbath day, but his constant residence was in some of those scattered houses that were in the wilderness of Zuph or Maon, which we read of in the story of David. There he spent most of his time, in contemplation and devotion, and had not his education in the schools, or at the feet of the rabbin. Note, Many a one is qualified for great usefulness, who yet is buried alive; and many are so long buried who are designed, and are thereby in the fitting, for so much greater usefulness at last; as John Baptist, who was <hi type="italic">in the desert</hi> only <hi type="italic">till the day of his showing to Israel,</hi> when he was in the thirtieth year of his age. Note, There is a time fixed for the <hi type="italic">showing</hi> of those favours to Israel which are reserved; <hi type="italic">the vision</hi> of them <hi type="italic">is for an appointed time, and at the end it shall speak, and shall not lie.</hi>  <chapter eID="Luke.1"/> <div eID="gen25220" type="x-p"/>

entries.f93e6786a70ca840a60ffce1677f02456e47af35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14207"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen27526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The writer of this Gospel is universally allowed to have been Lucas (an abbreviated form of Lucanus, as Silas of Silvanus), though he is not expressly named either in the Gospel or in the Acts. From <reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference> we learn that he was a "physician"; and by comparing that verse with <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.11">11</reference>--</hi>in which the apostle enumerates all those of the circumcision who were then with him, but does not mention Luke, though he immediately afterwards sends a salutation from him--we gather that Luke was not a born Jew. Some have thought he was a freed-man (libertinus), as the Romans devolved the healing art on persons of this class and on their slaves, as an occupation beneath themselves. His intimate acquaintance with Jewish customs, and his facility in Hebraic Greek, seem to show that he was an early convert to the Jewish faith; and this is curiously confirmed by <reference osisRef="Acts.21.27-Acts.21.29">Ac 21:27-29</reference>, where we find the Jews enraged at Paul's supposed introduction of Greeks into the temple, because they had seen "Trophimus the Ephesian" with him; and as we know that Luke was with Paul on that occasion, it would seem that they had taken him for a Jew, as they made no mention of him. On the other hand, his fluency in classical Greek confirms his Gentile origin. The time when he joined Paul's company is clearly indicated in the Acts by his changing (at <reference osisRef="Acts.16.10">Ac 16:10</reference>) from the third person singular ("he") to the first person plural ("we"). From that time he hardly ever left the apostle till near the period of his martyrdom (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>). Eusebius makes him a native of Antioch. If so, he would have every advantage for cultivating the literature of Greece and such medical knowledge as was then possessed. That he died a natural death is generally agreed among the ancients; Gregory Nazianzen alone affirming that he died a martyr.<div eID="gen27526" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27525" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27527" type="x-p"/> The time and place of the publication of his Gospel are alike uncertain. But we can approximate to it. It must at any rate have been issued before the Acts, for there the 'Gospel' is expressly referred to as the same author's "former treatise" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.1">Ac 1:1</reference>). Now the Book of the Acts was not published for two whole years after Paul's arrival as a prisoner at Rome, for it concludes with a reference to this period; but probably it was published soon after that, which would appear to have been early in the year 63. Before that time, then, we have reason to believe that the Gospel of Luke was in circulation, though the majority of critics make it later. If we date it somewhere between A.D. 50 and 60, we shall probably be near the truth; but nearer it we cannot with any certainty come. Conjectures as to the place of publication are too uncertain to be mentioned here.<div eID="gen27527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">That it was addressed, in the first instance, to Gentile readers, is beyond doubt. This is no more, as Davidson remarks [Introduction to the New Testament, p. 186], than was to have been expected from the companion of an "apostle of the Gentiles," who had witnessed marvellous changes in the condition of many heathens by the reception of the Gospel. But the explanations in his Gospel of things known to every Jew, and which could only be intended for Gentile readers, make this quite plain--</hi>see <reference osisRef="Luke.1.26">Lu 1:26</reference>; 4:31; 8:26; 21:37; 22:1; 24:13. A number of other minute particulars, both of things inserted and of things omitted, confirm the conclusion that it was Gentiles whom this Evangelist had in the first instance in view.<div eID="gen27528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We have already adverted to the classical style of Greek which this Evangelist writes--</hi>just what might have been expected from an educated Greek and travelled physician. But we have also observed that along with this he shows a wonderful flexibility of style, so much so, that when he comes to relate transactions wholly Jewish, where the speakers and actors and incidents are all Jewish, he writes in such Jewish Greek as one would do who had never been out of Palestine or mixed with any but Jews. In Da Costa's'S Four Witnesses will be found some traces of "the beloved physician" in this Gospel. But far more striking and important are the traces in it of his intimate connection with the apostle of the Gentiles. That one who was so long and so constantly in the society of that master mind has in such a work as this shown no traces of that connection, no stamp of that mind, is hardly to be believed. Writers of Introductions seem not to see it, and take no notice of it. But those who look into the interior of it will soon discover evidences enough in it of a Pauline cast of mind. Referring for a number of details to Da Costa, we notice here only two examples: <hi type="bold">In <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>, Paul ascribes to an express revelation from Christ Himself the account of the Institution of the Lord's Supper which he there gives. Now, if we find this account differing in small yet striking particulars from the accounts given by Matthew and Mark, but agreeing to the letter with Luke's account, it can hardly admit of a doubt that the one had it from the other; and in that case, of course, it was Luke that had it from Paul. Now Matthew and Mark both say of the Cup, "This is my blood of the New Testament"; while Paul and Luke say, in identical terms, "This cup is the New Testament in My blood" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">1Co 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.20">Lu 22:20</reference>). Further, Luke says, "Likewise also the cup after supper, saying," &c.; while Paul says, "After the same manner He took the cup when He had supped, saying," &c.; whereas neither Matthew nor Mark mention that this was after supper. But still more striking is another point of coincidence in this case. Matthew and Mark both say of the Bread merely this: "Take, eat; this is My body" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.26">Mt 26:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.22">Mr 14:22</reference>); whereas Paul says, "Take, eat, this is My body, which is broken for you" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.24">1Co 11:24</reference>), and Luke, "This is My body, which is given for you" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.19">Lu 22:19</reference>). And while Paul adds the precious clause, "This do in remembrance of Me," Luke does the same, in identical terms. How can one who reflects on this resist the conviction of a Pauline stamp in this Gospel? The other proof of this to which we ask the reader's attention is in the fact that Paul, in enumerating the parties by whom Christ was seen after His resurrection, begins, singularly enough, with Peter--</hi>"And that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures and that He was seen of Cephas, then of the Twelve" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.4">1Co 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.5">5</reference>)--coupled with the remarkable fact, that Luke is the only one of the Evangelists who mentions that Christ appeared to Peter at all. When the disciples had returned from Emmaus to tell their brethren how the Lord had appeared to them in the way, and how He had made Himself known to them in the breaking of bread, they were met, as Luke relates, ere they had time to utter a word, with this wonderful piece of news, "The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon" (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.34">Lu 24:34</reference>).<div eID="gen27529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27530" type="x-p"/> Other points connected with this Gospel will be adverted to in the Commentary.<div eID="gen27530" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <div sID="gen27531" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.1-Luke.1.4">Lu 1:1-4</reference>.<div eID="gen27531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27532" type="x-p"/> It appears from the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apostolic Epistles, that the earliest preaching of the Gospel consisted of a brief summary of the facts of our Lord's earthly history, with a few words of pointed application to the parties addressed. Of these astonishing facts, notes would naturally be taken and digests put into circulation. It is to such that Luke here refers; and in terms of studied respect, as narratives of what was "believed surely," or "on sure grounds" among Christians, and drawn up from the testimony of "eye-witnesses and ministering servants of the word." But when he adds that "it seemed good to him also to write in order, having traced down all things with exactness from their first rise," it is a virtual claim for his own Gospel to supersede these "many" narratives. Accordingly, while not one of them has survived the wreck of time, this and the other canonical Gospels live, and shall live, the only fitting vehicles of those life-bringing facts which have made all things new. Apocryphal or spurious gospels, upheld by parties unfriendly to the truths exhibited in the canonical Gospels, have not perished; but those well-meant and substantially correct narratives here referred to, used only while better were not to be had, were by tacit consent allowed to merge in the four peerless documents which from age to age, and with astonishing unanimity, have been accepted as the written charter of all Christianity.<div eID="gen27532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14207"/><hi type="bold">1. set forth in order--</hi>more simply, to draw up a narrative. <div eID="gen27533" type="x-p"/>
entries.400202f0e4d6c1784ecef6c29813af1888348059: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14208"/><div sID="gen27534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14208"/><hi type="bold">2. from the beginning--</hi>that is, of His public ministry, as is plain from what follows. <div eID="gen27534" type="x-p"/>
entries.77f608682cb9a90d48cd1b69220ffcb435ff3202: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14209"/><div sID="gen27535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14209"/><hi type="bold">3. from the very first--</hi>that is, from the very earliest events; referring to those precious details of the birth and early life, not only of our Lord, but of His forerunner, which we owe to Luke alone.<div eID="gen27535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in order--</hi>or "consecutively"--in contrast, probably, with the disjointed productions to which he had referred. But this must not be pressed too far; for, on comparing it with the other Gospels, we see that in some particulars the strict chronological order is not observed in this Gospel.<div eID="gen27536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">most excellent--</hi>or "most noble"--a title of rank applied by this same writer twice to Felix and once to Festus (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.26">Ac 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.3">24:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.25">26:25</reference>). It is likely, therefore, that "Theophilus" was chief magistrate of some city in Greece or Asia Minor [Webster and Wilkinson]. <div eID="gen27537" type="x-p"/>
entries.c87317f30c3eb3f7662e57600ec94717e657359f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14210"/><div sID="gen27538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14210"/><hi type="bold">4. that thou mightest know--</hi>"know thoroughly."<div eID="gen27538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hast been instructed--</hi>orally instructed--literally, "catechized" or "catechetically taught," at first as a catechumen or candidate for Christian baptism. <div eID="gen27539" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8c66a5d2cf03e685297f61456daa047c7cc34b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14211"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.1.5-Luke.1.25">Lu 1:5-25</reference>. Announcement of the Forerunner.</title> <div sID="gen27540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14211"/><hi type="bold">5. Herod--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.2.1">Mt 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen27540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">course of Abia--</hi>or Abijah; the eighth of the twenty-four orders of courses into which David divided the priests (see <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.1">1Ch 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.10">4, 10</reference>). Of these courses only four returned after the captivity (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.34-Ezra.2.39">Ezr 2:34-39</reference>), which were again subdivided into twenty-four--retaining the ancient name and order of each. They took the whole temple service for a week each.<div eID="gen27541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his wife was of the daughters of Aaron--</hi>The priests might marry into any tribe, but "it was most commendable of all to marry one of the priests' line" [Lightfoot]. <div eID="gen27542" type="x-p"/>
entries.69fbaa060cebe6f30ff9717008491c29d6022d20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14212"/><div sID="gen27543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14212"/><hi type="bold">6. commandments and ordinances--</hi>The one expressing their moral--the other their ceremonial--obedience [Calvin and Bengel], (Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.20">Eze 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.1">He 9:1</reference>). It has been denied that any such distinction was known to the Jews and New Testament writers. But <reference osisRef="Mark.12.33">Mr 12:33</reference>, and other passages, put this beyond all reasonable doubt. <div eID="gen27543" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8db319d0c9a51d261218113b8a952612bce0f6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14213"/><div sID="gen27544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14213"/>7. So with Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Elkanah and Hannah, Manoah and his wife. <div eID="gen27544" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1cca5ee54d9a162602ae772680066414b20c3aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14214"/><div sID="gen27545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14214"/><hi type="bold">9. his lot was to burn incense--</hi>The part assigned to each priest in his week of service was decided by lot. Three were employed at the offering of incense--to remove the ashes of the former service; to bring in and place on the golden altar the pan filled with hot burning coals taken from the altar of burnt offering; and to sprinkle the incense on the hot coals; and, while the smoke of it ascended, to make intercession for the people. This was the most distinguished part of the service (<reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Re 8:3</reference>), and this was what fell to the lot of Zacharias at this time [Lightfoot]. <div eID="gen27545" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6fa2fc4e7ebed78b62c8537ba52aecf4ad34e09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14215"/><div sID="gen27546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14215"/><hi type="bold">10. praying without--</hi>outside the court in front of the temple, where stood the altar of burnt offering; the men and women in separate courts, but the altar visible to all.<div eID="gen27546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the time of incense--</hi>which was offered along with the morning and evening sacrifice of every day; a beautiful symbol of the acceptableness of the sacrifice offered on the altar of burnt offering, with coals from whose altar the incense was burnt (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.12">Le 16:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.13">13</reference>). This again was a symbol of the "living sacrifice" of themselves and their services offered daily to God by the worshippers. Hence the language of <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Re 8:3</reference>. But that the acceptance of this daily offering depended on the expiatory virtue presupposed in the burnt offering, and pointing to the one "sacrifice of a sweet-smelling savor" (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>), is evident from <reference osisRef="Isa.6.6">Is 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.7">7</reference>. <div eID="gen27547" type="x-p"/>
entries.6776462dbf02851498a35374bbbf5790b3169932: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14216"/><div sID="gen27548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14216"/><hi type="bold">11. right side--</hi>the south side, between the altar and the candlestick, Zacharias being on the north side, in front of the altar, while offering incense [Webster and Wilkinson]. But why there? The right was the favorable side (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.33">Mt 25:33</reference>) [Schottgen and Westein in Meyer]; compare <reference osisRef="Mark.16.5">Mr 16:5</reference>. <div eID="gen27548" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b420f617154ece8cad2ee90c28f1a0f9f931ddd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14217"/><div sID="gen27549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14217"/><hi type="bold">13. thy prayer is heard--</hi>doubtless for offspring, which by some presentiment he even yet had not despaired of.<div eID="gen27549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">John--</hi>the same as "Johanan," so frequent in the Old Testament, meaning "Jehovah's gracious gift." <div eID="gen27550" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c7a0fca4f8afe0898b4a2159587bf9f30bd3fc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14218"/><div sID="gen27551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14218"/><hi type="bold">14. shall rejoice--</hi>so they did (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.58">Lu 1:58</reference>, 66); but the meaning rather is, "shall have cause to rejoice"--it would prove to many a joyful event. <div eID="gen27551" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1dd657479941e0ccf89ae302b21089fb918cc8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14219"/><div sID="gen27552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14219"/><hi type="bold">15. great in the sight of the Lord--</hi>nearer to Him in official standing than all the prophets. (See <reference osisRef="Matt.11.10">Mt 11:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.11">11</reference>.)<div eID="gen27552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drink neither wine nor strong drink--</hi>that is, shall be a Nazarite, or "a separated one" (<reference osisRef="Num.6.2">Nu 6:2</reference>, &c.). As the leper was the living symbol of sin, so was the Nazarite of holiness; nothing inflaming was to cross his lips; no razor to come on his head; no ceremonial defilement to be contracted. Thus was he to be "holy to the Lord [ceremonially] all the days of his separation." This separation was in ordinary cases temporary and voluntary: only Samson (<reference osisRef="Judg.13.7">Jud 13:7</reference>), Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.11">1Sa 1:11</reference>), and John Baptist were Nazarites from the womb. It was fitting that the utmost severity of legal consecration should be seen in Christ's forerunner. He was the Reality and Perfection of the Nazarite without the symbol, which perished in that living realization of it: "Such an High Priest became us, who was Separate from Sinners" (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.26">He 7:26</reference>).<div eID="gen27553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filled with the Holy Ghost, from ... womb--</hi>a holy vessel for future service. <div eID="gen27554" type="x-p"/>
entries.6affccf9a33a1a1e5b86c7ab8bfbbc7893b588bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14220"/><div sID="gen27555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14220"/><hi type="bold">16-17. A religious and moral reformer, Elijah-like, he should be (Mal 4:6, where the "turning of the people's heart to the Lord" is borrowed from <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.37">1Ki 18:37</reference>). In both cases their success, though great, was partial--</hi>the nation was not gained. <div eID="gen27555" type="x-p"/>
entries.220b150fa87bbda3192672d3e3c4cb691e677cd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14222"/><div sID="gen27561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14222"/><hi type="bold">18. Whereby, &c.--</hi>Mary believed what was far harder without a sign. Abraham, though older, and doubtless Sarah, too, when the same promise was made to him, "staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strong in faith, giving glory to God." This was that in which Zacharias failed. <div eID="gen27561" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfc97caae90e788ddf5dc64cfb2fef969c1151f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14223"/><div sID="gen27562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14223"/><hi type="bold">19. Gabriel--</hi>signifying "man of God," the same who appeared to Daniel at the time of incense (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Da 9:21</reference>) and to Mary (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.26">Lu 1:26</reference>).<div eID="gen27562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27563" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand, &c.--</hi>as his attendant (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.1">1Ki 17:1</reference>). <div eID="gen27563" type="x-p"/>
entries.f854297acf28c19acea664627534e86647d40ccf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14224"/><div sID="gen27564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14224"/><hi type="bold">20. dumb--</hi>speechless.<div eID="gen27564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not able--</hi>deprived of the power of speech (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.64">Lu 1:64</reference>). He asked a sign, and now he got it.<div eID="gen27565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">until the day that these things shall be performed--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Luke.1.64">Lu 1:64</reference>. <div eID="gen27566" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec699275b8257cac5c68e38d09cfc9c14ba05b6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14225"/><div sID="gen27567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14225"/><hi type="bold">21. waited--</hi>to receive from him the usual benediction (<reference osisRef="Num.6.23-Num.6.27">Nu 6:23-27</reference>).<div eID="gen27567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tarried so long--</hi>It was not usual to tarry long, lest it should be thought vengeance had stricken the people's representative for something wrong [Lightfoot]. <div eID="gen27568" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3dd785c45ab775aa3810500a1df84399f9d485d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14226"/><div sID="gen27569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14226"/><hi type="bold">22. speechless--</hi>dumb, and deaf also (see <reference osisRef="Luke.1.62">Lu 1:62</reference>). <div eID="gen27569" type="x-p"/>
entries.733634b7663356f597304489c34b3226be967f64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14227"/><div sID="gen27570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14227"/><hi type="bold">24. hid five months--</hi>till the event was put beyond doubt and became apparent.<div eID="gen27570" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.1.26-Luke.1.38">Lu 1:26-38</reference>. Annunciation of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen27571" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.18-Matt.1.21">Mt 1:18-21</reference>). <div eID="gen27571" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffff0c4f2900271e185aae13cdb2a38919a37503: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14228"/><div sID="gen27572" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14228"/><hi type="bold">26. sixth month--</hi>of Elisabeth's time.<div eID="gen27572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joseph, of the house of David--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.16">Mt 1:16</reference>). <div eID="gen27573" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a8ecff5f195d3f362fced6f275e89de640d3ac9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14229"/><div sID="gen27574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14229"/><hi type="bold">28. highly favoured--</hi>a word only once used elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>, "made accepted"): compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.30">Lu 1:30</reference>, "Thou hast found favour with God." The mistake of the Vulgate's rendering, "full of grace," has been taken abundant advantage of by the Romish Church. As the mother of our Lord, she was the most "blessed among women" in external distinction; but let them listen to the Lord's own words. "Nay, rather blessed are they that hear the word of God and keep it." (See on <reference osisRef="Luke.11.27">Lu 11:27</reference>). <div eID="gen27574" type="x-p"/>
entries.707c2d11f7ff70c9a19c6129bcaf3d03cd6d029a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14230"/><div sID="gen27575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14230"/>31. The angel purposely conforms his language to Isaiah's famous prophecy (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>) [Calvin]. <div eID="gen27575" type="x-p"/>
entries.5302d6cd416376a23d6183ac50f0932991c96f27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14231"/><div sID="gen27576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14231"/>32-33. This is but an echo of the sublime prediction in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">7</reference>. <div eID="gen27576" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dc5f9f6f9e007e6cc1ffc5672250baa0658de25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14232"/><div sID="gen27577" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14232"/><hi type="bold">34. How, &c.--</hi>not the unbelief of Zacharias, "Whereby shall I know this?" but, taking the fact for granted, "How is it to be, so contrary to the unbroken law of human birth?" Instead of reproof, therefore, her question is answered in mysterious detail. <div eID="gen27577" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d8f500f4864796f0010253850d9395c8bd876aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14233"/><div sID="gen27578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14233"/><hi type="bold">35. Holy Ghost--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.18">Mt 1:18</reference>).<div eID="gen27578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">power of the highest--</hi>the immediate energy of the Godhead conveyed by the Holy Ghost.<div eID="gen27579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overshadow--</hi>a word suggesting how gentle, while yet efficacious, would be this Power [Bengel]; and its mysterious secrecy, withdrawn, as if by a cloud, from human scrutiny [Calvin].<div eID="gen27580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that holy thing born of thee--</hi>that holy Offspring of thine.<div eID="gen27581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore ... Son of God--</hi>That Christ is the Son of God in His divine and eternal nature is clear from all the New Testament; yet here we see that Sonship efflorescing into human and palpable manifestation by His being born, through "the power of the Highest," an Infant of days. We must neither think of a double Sonship, as some do, harshly and without all ground, nor deny what is here plainly expressed, the connection between His human birth and His proper personal Sonship. <div eID="gen27582" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce70d43d04c530dd937f3b990778ae259c70cb03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14234"/><div sID="gen27583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14234"/><hi type="bold">36. thy cousin--</hi>"relative," but how near the word says not.<div eID="gen27583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">conceived, &c.--</hi>This was to Mary an unsought sign, in reward of her faith. <div eID="gen27584" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a85765d979b8ca86be3d69f1b9f9a51ecd2e9f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14235"/><div sID="gen27585" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14235"/><hi type="bold">37. For, &c.--</hi>referring to what was said by the angel to Abraham in like case (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.14">Ge 18:14</reference>), to strengthen her faith. <div eID="gen27585" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b83398c4608cd2e1f8eb95e2e71d2dc9c5ca39a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14236"/><div sID="gen27586" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14236"/>38. Marvellous faith in such circumstances! <div eID="gen27586" type="x-p"/>
entries.47b939d3494aead977e6f21720225bf1bae3ee7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14237"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.1.39-Luke.1.56">Lu 1:39-56</reference>. Visit of Mary to Elisabeth.</title> <div sID="gen27587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14237"/><hi type="bold">39. hill country--</hi>the mountainous tract running along the middle of Judea, from north to south [Webster and Wilkinson].<div eID="gen27587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with haste--</hi>transported with the announcement to herself and with the tidings, now first made known to her, of Elisabeth's condition.<div eID="gen27588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a city of Juda--</hi>probably Hebron (see <reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.11">21:11</reference>). <div eID="gen27589" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb2d5ce77f7875278c775df18e7590f14468285d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14238"/><div sID="gen27590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14238"/><hi type="bold">40. saluted Elisabeth--</hi>now returned from her seclusion (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.24">Lu 1:24</reference>). <div eID="gen27590" type="x-p"/>
entries.179a39a118f719ce96f32919dcd8d1c6f4aa469d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14239"/><div sID="gen27591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14239"/><hi type="bold">41. babe leaped--</hi>From <reference osisRef="Luke.1.44">Lu 1:44</reference> it is plain that this maternal sensation was something extraordinary--a sympathetic emotion of the unconscious babe, at the presence of the mother of his Lord. <div eID="gen27591" type="x-p"/>
entries.2054699fb3735a115462669259d20653a443d9f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14240"/><div sID="gen27592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14240"/>42-44. What beautiful superiority to envy have we here! High as was the distinction conferred upon herself, Elisabeth loses sight of it altogether, in presence of one more honored still; upon whom, with her unborn Babe, in an ecstasy of inspiration, she pronounces a benediction, feeling it to be a wonder unaccountable that "the mother of her Lord should come to her." "Turn this as we will, we shall never be able to see the propriety of calling an unborn child "Lord," but by supposing Elisabeth, like the prophets of old, enlightened to perceive the Messiah's Divine nature" [Olshausen]. <div eID="gen27592" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3ea5c54b5105eba068c5f5e27f9e91033e12039: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14242"/><div sID="gen27594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14242"/>45. An additional benediction on the Virgin for her implicit faith, in tacit and delicate contrast with her own husband.<div eID="gen27594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>rather, as in the Margin, "that." <div eID="gen27595" type="x-p"/>
entries.3432e70d918b802a85eedb19ba859cd09c8649d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14243"/><div sID="gen27596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14243"/><hi type="bold">46-55. A magnificent canticle, in which the strain of Hannah's ancient song, in like circumstances, is caught up, and just slightly modified and sublimed. Is it unnatural to suppose that the spirit of the blessed Virgin had been drawn beforehand into mysterious sympathy with the ideas and the tone of this hymn, so that when the life and fire of inspiration penetrated her whole soul it spontaneously swept the chorus of this song, enriching the Hymnal of the Church with that spirit-stirring canticle which has resounded ever since from its temple walls? In both songs, those holy women, filled with wonder to behold "the proud, the mighty, the rich," passed by, and, in their persons the lowliest chosen to usher in the greatest events, sing of this as no capricious movement, but a great law of the kingdom of God, by which He delights to "put down the mighty from their seats and exalt them of low degree." In both songs the strain dies away on Christ; in Hannah's under the name of "Jehovah's King"--</hi>to whom, through all His line, from David onwards to Himself, He will "give strength"; His "Anointed," whose horn He will exalt (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.10">1Sa 2:10</reference>); in the Virgin's song, it is as the "Help" promised to Israel by all the prophets.<div eID="gen27596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27597" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">My soul ... my spirit--</hi>"all that is within me" (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.1">Psa 103:1</reference>). <div eID="gen27597" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d8d9ebb52591ee6b2fca93366840d4e97f94202: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14247"/><div sID="gen27602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14247"/><hi type="bold">56. abode with her about three months--</hi>What an honored roof was that which, for such a period, overarched these cousins! and yet not a trace of it is now to be seen, while the progeny of those two women--the one but the honored pioneer of the other--have made the world new.<div eID="gen27602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">returned to her own house--</hi>at Nazareth, after which took place what is recorded in <reference osisRef="Matt.1.18-Matt.1.25">Mt 1:18-25</reference>. <div eID="gen27603" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c343eb525117ce92f81fc9c148fed8af2a9dd7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14248"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.1.57-Luke.1.80">Lu 1:57-80</reference>. Birth and Circumcision of John--Song of Zacharias and Progress of the Child.</title> <div sID="gen27604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14248"/><hi type="bold">59. eighth day--</hi>The law (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.12">Ge 17:12</reference>) was observed, even though the eighth day after birth should be a sabbath (<reference osisRef="John.7.23">Joh 7:23</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Php 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen27604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called him--</hi>literally, "were calling"--that is, (as we should say) "were for calling." The naming of children at baptism has its origin in the Jewish custom at circumcision (<reference osisRef="Gen.21.3">Ge 21:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.4">4</reference>); and the names of Abram and Sarai were changed at its first performance (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.5">Ge 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen27605" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ede49dbf31f36e33b7068bab826c9e160bd96ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14249"/><div sID="gen27606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14249"/><hi type="bold">62. made signs--</hi>showing he was deaf, as well as dumb. <div eID="gen27606" type="x-p"/>
entries.32d01c3b3082b5b67580184077e2164c953cf9f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14250"/><div sID="gen27607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14250"/><hi type="bold">63. marvelled all--</hi>at his giving the same name, not knowing of any communication between them on the subject. <div eID="gen27607" type="x-p"/>
entries.6dc061121b05b94ae595c5c24f6eebc0a3a2835b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14251"/><div sID="gen27608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14251"/><hi type="bold">64. mouth opened immediately--</hi>on thus palpably showing his full faith in the vision, for disbelieving which he had been struck dumb (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.13">Lu 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen27608" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d54a6eacc6675c71eb6ba77f475ab2774ec4a73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14252"/><div sID="gen27609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14252"/><hi type="bold">65. fear--</hi>religious awe; under the impression that God's hand was specially in these events (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.5.26">Lu 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.7.16">7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.37">8:37</reference>). <div eID="gen27609" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f79bf528eabcae872cbefe338acfb0f973f8e75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14253"/><div sID="gen27610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14253"/><hi type="bold">66. hand of the Lord was with him--</hi>by special tokens marking him out as one destined to some great work (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.46">1Ki 18:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.15">2Ki 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.11.21">Ac 11:21</reference>). <div eID="gen27610" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0b5271fc70d13518b499d5aa3948e6f97a24c89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14254"/><div sID="gen27611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14254"/>68-79. There is not a word in this noble burst of divine song about his own child; like Elisabeth losing sight entirely of self, in the glory of a Greater than both.<div eID="gen27611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord God of Israel--</hi>the ancient covenant God of the peculiar people.<div eID="gen27612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visited and redeemed--</hi>that is, in order to redeem: returned after long absence, and broken His long silence (see <reference osisRef="Matt.15.31">Mt 15:31</reference>). In the Old Testament, God is said to "visit" chiefly for judgment, in the New Testament for mercy. Zacharias would, as yet, have but imperfect views of such "visiting and redeeming," "saving from and delivering out of the hand of enemies" (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.71">Lu 1:71</reference>, 74). But this Old Testament phraseology, used at first with a lower reference, is, when viewed in the light of a loftier and more comprehensive kingdom of God, equally adapted to express the most spiritual conceptions of the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen27613" type="x-p"/>
entries.95d9a5e567cc198e09626a4e06bacefbc0cbeabf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14264"/><div sID="gen27628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14264"/><hi type="bold">80. And the child, &c.--</hi>"a concluding paragraph, indicating, in strokes full of grandeur, the bodily and mental development of the Baptist; and bringing his life up to the period of his public appearance" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen27628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the deserts--</hi>probably "the wilderness of Judea" (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.1">Mt 3:1</reference>), whither he had retired early in life, in the Nazarite spirit, and where, free from rabbinical influences and alone with God, his spirit would be educated, like Moses in the desert, for his future high vocation.<div eID="gen27629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his showing unto Israel--</hi>the presentation of himself before his nation, as Messiah's forerunner. <chapter eID="Luke.1"/>

entries.8bd2f1cec511b4f5c04ac0ea9a08babf67a04796: <div eID="gen39739" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Gospel According to St. Luke With a Short Account of His Life</title> <div sID="gen39740" type="x-p"/> There is little certain known of this evangelist: from what is spoken in the Scriptures, and by the best informed of the primitive fathers, the following probable account is collected: - <div eID="gen39740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39741" type="x-p"/> Luke was, according to Dr. Lardner, a Jew by birth, and an early convert to Christianity; but Michaelis thinks he was a Gentile, and brings <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.11">Col 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference>, in proof, where St. Paul distinguished Aristarchus, Marcus, and Jesus, who was called Justus, from Epaphras, Lucas, and Demas, who were of the circumcision, i.e. Jews. Some think he was one of our Lord's seventy disciples. It is worthy of remark that he is the only evangelist who mentions the commission given by Christ to the seventy, Luke 10:1-20. It is likely he is the Lucius mentioned <reference osisRef="Rom.16.21">Rom 16:21</reference>, and if so he was related to the Apostle Paul, and that it is the same Lucius of Cyrene who is mentioned <reference osisRef="Act.13.1">Act 13:1</reference>, and in general with others, <reference osisRef="Act.11.20">Act 11:20</reference>. Some of the ancients, and some of the most learned and judicious among the moderns, think he was one of the two whom our Lord met on the way to Emmaus on the day of his resurrection, as related Luke 24:13-35; one of these was called Cleopas, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.18">Luk 24:18</reference>, the other is not mentioned, the evangelist, himself, being the person and the relator. <div eID="gen39741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39742" type="x-p"/> St. Paul styles him his fellow-laborer, <reference osisRef="Plm.1.24">Plm 1:24</reference>. It is barely probable that he is the person mentioned, <reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference>, Luke, the beloved physician. All the ancients of repute, such as Eusebius, Gregory Nyssen, Jerome, Paulinus, Euthalius, Euthymius, and others, agree that he was a physician, but where he was born, and where he exercised the duties of his profession, are not known. Many moderns have attributed to him the most profound skill in the science of painting, and that he made some pictures of the Virgin Mary. This is justly esteemed fabulous; nor is this science attributed to him by any writer previously to Nicephorus Callisti, in the fourteenth century, an author who scarcely deserves any credit, especially in relations not confirmed by others. <div eID="gen39742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39743" type="x-p"/> He accompanied St. Paul when he first went into Macedonia, Acts 16:8-40; <reference osisRef="Act.20.1">Act 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.27.1">Act 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.28.1">Act 28:1</reference>. Whether he went with him constantly afterwards is not certain; but it is evident he accompanied him from Greece through Macedonia and Asia to Jerusalem, where he is supposed to have collected many particulars of the evangelic history: from Jerusalem he went with Paul to Rome, where he stayed with him the two years of his imprisonment in that city. This alone makes out the space of five years, and upwards. It is probable that he left St. Paul when he was set at liberty, and that he then went into Greece, where he finished and published this Gospel, and the book of the Acts, which he dedicated to Theophilus, an honorable Christian friend of his in that country. It is supposed that he died in peace about the eightieth or eighty-fourth year of his age. Some suppose he published this Gospel fifteen, others twenty-two years after the ascension of Christ. <div eID="gen39743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39744" type="x-p"/> See much on this subject in Lardner, Works, vol. vi. p. 104, etc., and in Michaelis's Introduction to the New Testament. <div eID="gen39744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39745" type="x-p"/> Some learned men think that Luke has borrowed considerably from St. Matthew: collate <reference osisRef="Luk.3.7-Luk.3.9">Luk 3:7-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.16">Luk 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.17">Luk 3:17</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Mat.3.7-Mat.3.12">Mat 3:7-12</reference>; also Luke 5:20-38, with Matthew 9:2-17; also <reference osisRef="Luk.6.1-Luk.6.5">Luk 6:1-5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Mat.12.1-Mat.12.5">Mat 12:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.7.22-Luk.7.28">Luk 7:22-28</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Mat.11.4-Mat.11.11">Mat 11:4-11</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Luk.12.22-Luk.12.31">Luk 12:22-31</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Mat.6.25-Mat.6.33">Mat 6:25-33</reference>. It is allowed that there is considerable diversity in the order of time between St Matthew and St. Luke, which is accounted for thus: Matthew deduces the facts related in his history in chronological order. Luke, on the contrary, appears to have paid little attention to this order, because he proposed to make a classification of events, referring each to its proper class, without paying any attention to chronological arrangement. Some critics divide this history into five distinct classes or sections, in the following manner: - <div eID="gen39745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39746" type="x-p"/> CLASS I. Comprehends all the details relative to the birth of Christ; with the preceding, concomitant, and immediately succeeding circumstances. <reference osisRef="Luk.1.1">Luk 1:1</reference>, and 2:1-40. <div eID="gen39746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39747" type="x-p"/> CLASS II. Contains a description of our Lord's infancy and bringing up; his visit to the temple when twelve years of age; and his going down to Nazareth and continuing under the government of his parents; <reference osisRef="Luk.2.41-Luk.2.52">Luk 2:41-52</reference>. <div eID="gen39747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39748" type="x-p"/> CLASS III. Contains the account of the preaching of John Baptist, and his success; the baptism of Christ, and his genealogy. <reference osisRef="Luk.3.1">Luk 3:1</reference>. <div eID="gen39748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39749" type="x-p"/> CLASS IV. Comprehends the account of all our Lord's transactions in Galilee, for the whole three years of his ministry, from <reference osisRef="Luk.4.1">Luk 4:1</reference> to Luke 9:1-50. This seems evident: for as soon as Luke had given the account of our Lord's temptation in the deserts <reference osisRef="Luk.4.1-Luk.4.13">Luk 4:1-13</reference>, he represents him as immediately returning in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, <reference osisRef="Luk.4.14">Luk 4:14</reference>; mentions Nazareth, <reference osisRef="Luk.4.16">Luk 4:16</reference>; Capernaum, <reference osisRef="Luk.4.31">Luk 4:31</reference>; and the lake of Galilee, <reference osisRef="Luk.5.1">Luk 5:1</reference>; and thus, to <reference osisRef="Luk.9.50">Luk 9:50</reference>, goes on to describe the preaching, miracles, etc.; of our Lord in Galilee. <div eID="gen39749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39750" type="x-p"/> CLASS V. and last, commences at <reference osisRef="Luk.9.51">Luk 9:51</reference>, where the evangelist gives an account of our Lord's last journey to Jerusalem: therefore this class contains, not only all the transactions of our Lord from that time to his crucifixion, but also, the account of his resurrection, his commission to his apostles, and his ascension to heaven. <reference osisRef="Luk.9.51">Luk 9:51</reference>, to <reference osisRef="Luk.24.53">Luk 24:53</reference>, inclusive. <div eID="gen39750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39751" type="x-p"/> A plan similar to this has been followed by Suetonius, in his life of Augustus: he does not produce his facts in chronological order, but classifies them, as he himself professes, cap. 12, giving an account of all his wars, honors, legislative acts, discipline, domestic life, etc., etc. Matthew therefore, is to be consulted for the correct arrangement of facts in chronological order: Luke, for a classification of facts and events, without any attention to the order of time in which they occurred. Many eminent historians have conducted their narratives in the same way. See Rosenmuller. It must not, however, be forgotten, that this evangelist gives us some very valuable chronological data in several parts of the three first chapters. These shall be noticed in their proper places. <div eID="gen39751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39752" type="x-p"/> The preface, or St. Luke's private epistle to Theophilus, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.1-Luk.1.4">Luk 1:1-4</reference>. The conception and birth of John Baptist foretold by the angel Gabriel, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.5-Luk.1.17">Luk 1:5-17</reference>. Zacharias doubts, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.18">Luk 1:18</reference>. And the angel declares he shall be dumb, till the accomplishment of the prediction, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.19-Luk.1.25">Luk 1:19-25</reference>. Six months after the angel Gabriel appears to the virgin Mary, and predicts the miraculous conception and birth of Christ, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.26-Luk.1.38">Luk 1:26-38</reference>. Mary visits her cousin Elisabeth, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.39-Luk.1.45">Luk 1:39-45</reference>. Mary's song of exultation and praise, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.46-Luk.1.56">Luk 1:46-56</reference>. John the Baptist is born, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.57-Luk.1.66">Luk 1:57-66</reference>. The prophetic song of his father Zacharias, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.67-Luk.1.79">Luk 1:67-79</reference>. John is educated in the desert, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.80">Luk 1:80</reference>. <div eID="gen39752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39753" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39754" type="x-p"/> Many have taken in hand - Great and remarkable characters have always many biographers. So it appears it was with our Lord: but as most of these accounts were inaccurate, recording as facts things which had not happened; and through ignorance or design mistaking others, especially in the place where St. Luke wrote; it seemed good to the Holy Spirit to inspire this holy man with the most correct knowledge of the whole history of our Lord's birth, preaching, miracles, sufferings, death, resurrection, and ascension, that the sincere, upright followers of God might have a sure foundation, on which they might safely build their faith. See the note on <reference osisRef="Luk.9.10">Luk 9:10</reference>. <div eID="gen39754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39755" type="x-p"/> Most surely believed among us - Facts confirmed by the fullest evidence - των πεπληροφορημενων πραγματων. Every thing that had been done or said by Jesus Christ was so public, so plain, and so accredited by thousands of witnesses, who could have had no interest in supporting an imposture, as to carry the fullest conviction, to the hearts of those who heard and saw him, of the divinity of his doctrine, and the truth of his miracles.
entries.15541d9e7f135204bd4423e4801d93128dc65489: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39756" type="x-p"/> Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eye-witnesses - Probably this alludes to the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, which it is likely were written before St. Luke wrote his, and on the models of which he professes to write his own; and απ' αρχης, from the beginning, must mean, from the time that Christ first began to proclaim the glad tidings of the kingdom; and αυτοπται, eye-witnesses, must necessarily signify, those who had been with him from the beginning, and consequently had the best opportunities of knowing the truth of every fact. <div eID="gen39756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39757" type="x-p"/> Ministers of the word - Του λογου. Some suppose that our blessed Lord is meant by this phrase; as ὁ Λογος, the Word or Logos, is his essential character in <reference osisRef="Joh.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>, etc.; but it does not appear that any of the inspired penmen ever use the word in this sense except John himself; for here it certainly means the doctrine of Christ; and in this sense λογος is frequently used both by the evangelists and apostles.
entries.eaac408465132537d821fe127835e3e57b3f535a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39758" type="x-p"/> Having had perfect understanding - Παρηκολουθηκοτι ανωθεν, Having accurately traced up - entered into the very spirit of the work, and examined every thing to the bottom; in consequence of which investigation, I am completely convinced of the truth of the whole. Though God gives his Holy Spirit to all them who ask him, yet this gift was never designed to set aside the use of those faculties with which he has already endued the soul, and which are as truly his gifts as the Holy Spirit itself is. The nature of inspiration, in the case of St. Luke, we at once discover: he set himself, by impartial inquiry and diligent investigation, to find the whole truth, and to relate nothing but the truth; and the Spirit of God presided over and directed his inquiries, so that he discovered the whole truth, and was preserved from every particle of error. <div eID="gen39758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39759" type="x-p"/> From the very first - Ανωθεν, from their origin. Some think ανωθεν should, in this place, be translated from above; and that it refers to the inspiration by which St. Luke wrote. I prefer our translation, or, from the origin, which several good critics contend for, and which meaning it has in some of the best Greek writers. See Kypke. <div eID="gen39759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39760" type="x-p"/> Theophilus - As the literal import of this word is friend of God, Θεου φιλος, some have supposed that under this name Luke comprised all the followers of Christ, to whom, as friends of God, he dedicated this faithful history of the life, doctrine, death, and resurrection of our Lord. But this interpretation appears to have little solidity in it; for, if all the followers of Christ are addressed, why is the singular number used? and what good end could there be accomplished by using a feigned name? Besides, κρατιϚε, most excellent, could never be applied in this way, for it evidently designates a particular person, and one probably distinguished by his situation in life; though this does not necessarily follow from the title, which was often given in the way of friendship. Theophilus appears to have been some very reputable Greek or Roman, who was one of St. Luke's disciples. The first four verses seem a private epistle, sent by the evangelist with this history, which, having been carefully preserved by Theophilus, was afterwards found and published with this Gospel.
entries.29dfc4c6ff7bfdef7f36c4f851ceb157cc7b459a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39761" type="x-p"/> Wherein thou hast been instructed - Κατηχηθης - In which thou hast been catechized. It appears that Theophilus had already received the first elements of the Christian doctrine, but had not as yet been completely grounded in them. That he might know the certainty of the things in which he had been thus catechized, by having all the facts and their proofs brought before him in order, the evangelist sent him this faithful and Divinely inspired narrative. Those who content themselves with that knowledge of the doctrines of Christ which they receive from catechisms and schoolmasters, however important these elementary instructions may be, are never likely to arrive at such a knowledge of the truth as will make them wise unto salvation, or fortify them against the attacks of infidelity and irreligion. Every man should labor to acquire the most correct knowledge, and indubitable certainty, of those doctrines on which he stakes his eternal salvation. Some suppose that St. Luke refers here to the imperfect instruction which Theophilus had received from the defective Gospels to which he refers in <reference osisRef="Luk.1.1">Luk 1:1</reference>.
entries.600db04f69109ace0be1a71745e2042aea751b67: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen39761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39762" type="x-p"/> In the days of Herod, the king - This was Herod, surnamed the Great, the son of Antipater, an Idumean by birth, who had professed himself a proselyte to the Jewish religion, but regarded no religion, farther than it promoted his secular interests and ambition. Thus, for the first time, the throne of Judah was filled by a person not of Jewish extraction, who had been forced upon the people by the Roman government. Hence it appears plain that the prophecy of Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, was now fulfilled; for the scepter had departed from Judah: and now was the time, according to another prophecy, to look for the governor from Bethlehem, who should rule and feed the people of Israel: <reference osisRef="Mic.5.1">Mic 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic 5:2</reference>. See a large account of the family of the Herods, in the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.2.1">Mat 2:1</reference> (note). This was before Christ six years. <div eID="gen39762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39763" type="x-p"/> The course of Abiah - When the sacerdotal families grew very numerous, so that all could not officiate together at the tabernacle, David divided them into twenty-four classes, that they might minister by turns, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.1">1Chr 24:1</reference>, etc., each family serving a whole week, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.7">2Kgs 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.8">2Chr 23:8</reference>. Abiah was the eighth in the order in which they had been originally established: <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.10">1Chr 24:10</reference>. These dates and persons are particularly mentioned as a full confirmation of the truth of the facts themselves; because any person, at the time this Gospel was written, might have satisfied himself by applying to the family of John the Baptist, the family of our Lord, or the surrounding neighbors. What a full proof of the Gospel history! It was published immediately after the time in which these facts took place; and among the very people, thousands of whom had been eye-witnesses of them; and among those, too, whose essential interest it was to have discredited them if they could; and yet, in all that age, in which only they could have been contradicted with advantage, no man ever arose to call them in question! What an absolute proof was this that the thing was impossible; and that the truth of the Gospel history was acknowledged by all who paid any attention to the evidences it produced! <div eID="gen39763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39764" type="x-p"/> Of the daughters of Aaron - That is, she was of one of the sacerdotal families. This shows that John was most nobly descended: his father was a priest and his mother the daughter of a priest; and thus, both by father and mother, he descended from the family of Amram, of whom came Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, the most illustrious characters in the whole Jewish history.
entries.22efa6ff07d98ba11a940ce75d7f79525800fccc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen39764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39765" type="x-p"/> They were both righteous - Upright and holy in all their outward conduct in civil life. <div eID="gen39765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39766" type="x-p"/> Before God - Possessing the spirit of the religion they professed; exercising themselves constantly in the presence of their Maker, whose eye, they knew, was upon all their conduct, and who examined all their motives. <div eID="gen39766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39767" type="x-p"/> Walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless - None being able to lay any evil to their charge. They were as exemplary and conscientious in the discharge of their religious duties as they were in the discharge of the offices of civil life. What a sacred pair! they made their duty to God, to their neighbor, and to themselves, walk constantly hand in hand. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.15">Mat 3:15</reference>. Perhaps εντολαι, commandments, may here mean the decalogue; and δικαιωματα, ordinances, the ceremonial and judicial laws which were delivered after the decalogue: as all the precepts delivered from <reference osisRef="Exo.21.1">Exo 21:1</reference> to <reference osisRef="Exo.24.1">Exo 24:1</reference> are termed δικαιωματα, judgments or ordinances.
entries.20582abfeb4dd16ab75ecdd109dcb7a253e1fa6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39768" type="x-p"/> Both were now well stricken in years - By the order of God, sterility and old age both met in the person of Elisabeth, to render the birth of a son (humanly speaking) impossible. This was an exact parallel to the case of Sarah and Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.11.30">Gen 11:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.17.17">Gen 17:17</reference>. Christ must (by the miraculous power of God) be born of a virgin: whatever was connected with, or referred to, his incarnation must be miraculous and impressive. Isaac was his grand type, and therefore must be born miraculously - contrary to the common course and rule of nature: Abraham was a hundred years of age, Sarah was ninety, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.17">Gen 17:17</reference>, and it had Ceased to be with Sarah After The Manner Of Women, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.11">Gen 18:11</reference>, and therefore, from her age and state, the birth of a child must, according to nature, have been impossible; and it was thus; that it might be miraculous. John the Baptist was to be the forerunner of Christ; his birth, like that of Isaac, must be miraculous, because, like the other, it was to be a representation of the birth of Christ; therefore his parents were both far advanced in years, and besides, Elisabeth was naturally barren. The birth of these three extraordinary persons was announced nearly in the same way. God himself foretells the birth of Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.16">Gen 17:16</reference>. The angel of the Lord announces the birth of John the Baptist, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.13">Luk 1:13</reference>; and six months after, the angel Gabriel, the same angel, proclaims to Mary the birth of Christ! Man is naturally an inconsiderate and incredulous creature: he must have extraordinary things to arrest and fix his attention; and he requires well-attested miracles from God, to bespeak and confirm his faith. Every person who has properly considered the nature of man must see that the whole of natural religion, so termed, is little else than a disbelief of all religion.
entries.c9ff4b8dfe49e918dad75b3e484c0155f6c6c50e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39769" type="x-p"/> Before God - In the temple, where God used to manifest his presence, though long before this time he had forsaken it; yet, on this important occasion, the angel of his presence had visited it.
entries.579df399457d932b9a1835a07e53e67f219dffdc: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39770" type="x-p"/> His lot was, etc. - We are informed in the Talmud, that it was the custom of the priests to divide the different functions of the sacerdotal office among themselves by lot: and, in this case, the decision of the lot was, that Zacharias should at that time burn the incense before the Lord, in the holy place.
entries.680021379e30840e44613c4e502f5224ae751412: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen39770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39771" type="x-p"/> The whole multitude - were praying - The incense was itself an emblem of the prayers and praises of the people of God: see <reference osisRef="Psa.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.1">Rev 8:1</reference>. While, therefore, the rite is performing by the priest, the people are employed in the thing signified. Happy the people who attend to the spirit as well as the letter of every divine institution! Incense was burnt twice a day in the temple, in the morning and in the evening, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.7">Exo 30:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.30.8">Exo 30:8</reference>; but the evangelist does not specify the time of the day in which this transaction took place. It was probably in the morning.
entries.4ee0c412a32aab3a38ae818e0cc94421bbb0eae1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen39771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39772" type="x-p"/> There appeared - an angel of the Lord - There had been neither prophecy nor angelic ministry vouchsafed to this people for about 400 years. But now, as the Sun of righteousness is about to arise upon them, the day-spring from on high visits them, that they may be prepared for that kingdom of God which was at hand. Every circumstance here is worthy of remark: <div eID="gen39772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39773" type="x-p"/> 1. That an angel should now appear, as such a favor had not been granted for 400 years. <div eID="gen39773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39774" type="x-p"/> 2. The person to whom this angel was sent - one of the priests. The sacerdotal office itself pointed out the Son of God till he came: by him it was to be completed, and in him it was to be eternally established: - Thou art a priest for ever, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>. <div eID="gen39774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39775" type="x-p"/> 3. The place in which the angel appeared - Jerusalem; out of which the word of the Lord should go forth, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference>, and not at Hebron, in the hill country of Judea, where Zacharias lived, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.39">Luk 1:39</reference>, which was the ordinary residence of the priests, <reference osisRef="Jos.21.11">Jos 21:11</reference>, where there could have been few witnesses of this interposition of God, and the effects produced by it. <div eID="gen39775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39776" type="x-p"/> 4. The place where he was when the angel appeared to him - in the temple, which was the place where God was to be sought; the place of his residence, and a type of the human nature of the blessed Jesus, <reference osisRef="Joh.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>. <div eID="gen39776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39777" type="x-p"/> 5.
