If his bare promises do not satisfy us, let us at least remember this confirmation of them; and if it does not remove all doubt, we are chargeable with heinous ingratitude to God, and insult to his holy name.<div eID="gen96036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96037" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To give to us</hi> Zacharias does not enumerate the several points of God’s covenant, but shows that God’s purpose, in dealing so kindly and mercifully with his people, was to redeem them.<div eID="gen96037" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.73" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96035" osisID="Luke.1.73" type="section"/>
entries.d90bc78027cc20daf7cc15746a3865bd1cb0389c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.74" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.1.74" sID="gen96038" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">74. </hi><hi type="italic">That being delivered out of the hand of our enemies</hi> His purpose was, that, being redeemed, they might dedicate and consecrate themselves entirely to the Author of their salvation. As the efficient cause of human salvation was the undeserved goodness of God, so its final cause is, that, by a godly and holy life, men may glorify his name. This deserves careful attention, that we may remember our calling, and so learn to apply the grace of God to its proper use. We must meditate on such declarations as these:<div eID="gen96039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96040" type="x-p"/>“God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness,” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Thess.4.7">1 Thessalonians 4:7</reference>.)<div eID="gen96040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96041" type="x-p"/>We are “redeemed with a great price,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.20">1 Corinthians 6:20</reference>,) “the precious blood of Christ,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.18 Bible:1Pet.1.19">1 Peter 1:18,19</reference>,) not that we may serve “the lusts of the flesh,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Pet.2.18">2 Peter 2:18</reference>,) or indulge in unbridled licentiousness, but that Christ may reign in us. We are admitted by adoption into the family of God, that we, on our part, may yield obedience as children to a father. For “the kindness and love (<foreign xml:lang="el">φιλανθρωπία</foreign>) of God our Savior toward man,” (<reference osisRef="">Titus 3:4</reference>,) “hath appeared unto all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly,” (<reference osisRef="">Titus 2:11,12</reference>.) And so Paul, when he wishes powerfully to exhort believers to consecrate themselves to God, “in newness of life,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.4">Romans 6:4</reference>,) and, “putting off, concerning the former conversation, the old man,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.22">Ephesians 4:22</reference>,) to render to him a “reasonable service,” “beseeches them by the mercies of God,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.1">Romans 12:1</reference>.) Scripture is full of declarations of this nature, which show that we “frustrate the grace” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.21">Galatians 2:21</reference>) of Christ, if we do not follow out this design.<div eID="gen96041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96042" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That we may serve him without fear</hi> This deserves our attention: for it implies that we cannot worship God in a proper manner without composure of mind. Those who are ill at ease, who have an inward struggle, whether God is favorable or hostile to them, whether he accepts or rejects their services,—in a word, who fluctuate in uncertainty between hope and fear, will sometimes labor anxiously in the worship of God, but never will sincerely or honestly obey him. Alarm and dread make them turn from him with horror; and so, if it were possible, they would desire that there were, “no God,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.14.1">Psalm 14:1</reference>.) But we know, that no sacrifice is acceptable to God, which is not offered willingly, and with a cheerful heart. Before men can truly worship <hi type="italic">God, </hi>they must obtain peace of conscience, as David speaks, “There is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.130.4">Psalm 130:4</reference>:) for those to whom God has given peace are graciously invited and led to approach him willingly and with a cheerful desire to worship him. Hence too Paul deduces that maxim, that “whatsoever is undertaken without faith is sin,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.14.23">Romans 14:23</reference>.) But since God reconciles men to himself in Christ, since by his protection he keeps them safe from all fear, since he has committed their salvation to his own hand and guardianship, we are justly declared by Zacharias to be delivered by his grace from fear. And so the prophets describe it as peculiar to his reign, that,<div eID="gen96042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96043" type="x-p"/>“they shall sit every man under his vine, and under his fig-tree, and none shall make them afraid,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mic.4.4">Micah 4:4</reference>.)<div eID="gen96043" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.74" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96038" osisID="Luke.1.74" type="section"/>
entries.e78468596871cbcc6a3282b7051d9561cdb4833a:
75. In holiness and righteousness As the rule of a good life has been reduced by God to two tables, (Exodus 31:18; 34:1,) so Zacharias here declares, that we serve God in a proper manner, when our life has been framed to holiness and righteousness. Holiness, beyond all question, denotes—as even Plato knew the duties of godliness,
“Le mot de Sainctete comprend tout ce dont nous sommes redevables a Dieu pour adorer et honorer sa majeste.” — “The word Holiness includes all that we owe to God for adoring and honoring his majesty.”
which relate to the first table of the law. Righteousness, again, extends to all the duties of charity: for God requires nothing more from us in the second table of the law, than to render to every one what belongs to him. It is added, before him, to instruct believers, that it is not enough if their lives are decently regulated before the eyes of men, and their hands, and feet, and whole body, restrained from every kind of open wickedness: but they must live according to the will of God, who is not satisfied with professions of holiness, but looks chiefly on the heart.
Lastly, That no man may consider his duties to be at an end, when he has worshipped God for a certain period, Zacharias declares that men have been redeemed on the condition
“Hac lege redemptas esse homines.” — “Zacharie dit que les hommes ont este rachetez a la charge de s'appliquer a servir Dieu tout le temps de leur vie.” — “Zacharias says that men have been redeemed upon condition of applying themselves to serve God all the time of their life.”
that they shall continue to devote themselves to the worship of God all the days of their life And certainly, as redemption is eternal, the remembrance of it ought never to pass away; as God adopts men into his family for ever, their gratitude ought not to be transitory or of short continuance; and, in a word, as “Christ both died and rose, and revived” for them, it is proper that he should be “Lord both of the dead and living,” (Romans 14:9.) So Paul, in a passage which I lately quoted, enjoins us to
“live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world; looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ; who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works,” (Titus 2:12-14.)
LUKE 1:76-80
Luke 1:76-80
76. And thou, child, shalt be called the Prophet of the Highest. for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, 77. To give knowledge of salvation to his people by the forgiveness of their sins: 78. Through the bowels of the mercy of our God, by which the Eastern sky
“Oriens ex alto.”
hath visited us, 79. That he might give light to those who were sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace. 80. And the child grew, and became strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his showing unto Israel.
entries.270616773183b822cd6bf17a763df9d125e92cac: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.76" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.1.76" sID="gen96056" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">76.</hi> <hi type="italic">And thou, child</hi> Zacharias again returns to commend the grace of Christ, but does this, as it were, in the person of his son, by describing briefly the office to which he had been appointed as an instructor. Though in a little infant eight days old he does not yet observe prophetical endowments, yet turning his eyes to the purpose of God, he speaks of it as a thing already known. <hi type="italic">To be called</hi> means here to be <hi type="italic">considered and openly acknowledged</hi> as the prophet of God. A secret calling of God had already taken place. It only remained that the nature of that calling should be manifested to men. But as the name <hi type="italic">Prophet </hi>is general, Zacharias, following the revelation brought to him by the angel, affirms that he would be the usher <note n="80"> <div sID="gen96058" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Apparitorem</foreign>.” — “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Heraut</foreign>.”<div eID="gen96058" type="x-p"/> </note> or herald of Christ. He says, <hi type="italic">thou shalt go before the face of the Lord: </hi>that is, thou shalt discharge the office of turning men by thy preaching to hear the Lord. The reason why John, when he had nearly finished his course, affirmed that he was not a <hi type="italic">prophet </hi>of God, is explained by me at the proper place, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.21">John 1:21</reference>,) and in what manner he was <hi type="italic">to prepare his ways</hi> we shall afterwards see.<div eID="gen96057" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.76" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96056" osisID="Luke.1.76" type="section"/>
entries.052b94948642a2962f6c31b34e54b64f6c09d782: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.77" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.1.77" sID="gen96059" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">77.</hi> <hi type="italic">To give knowledge of salvation</hi> Zacharias now touches the principal subject of the gospel, when he says that the <hi type="italic">knowledge of salvation</hi> consists in <hi type="italic">the forgiveness of sins</hi>. As we are all “by nature the children of wraths” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.3">Ephesians 2:3</reference>,) it follows, that we are by nature condemned and ruined: and the ground of our condemnation is, that we are chargeable with unrighteousness. There is, therefore, no other provision for escaping eternal death <note n="81"> <div sID="gen96061" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Mortis</foreign><hi type="italic">;” </hi>—<hi type="italic"> “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr">La mort mortelle</foreign>.”<div eID="gen96061" type="x-p"/> </note> but by God<div eID="gen96060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96062" type="x-p"/>“reconciling us unto himself, not imputing our trespasses unto us,” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.19">2 Corinthians 5:19</reference>.)<div eID="gen96062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96063" type="x-p"/>That this is the only righteousness which remains to us before God, may be easily gathered from the words of Zacharias. For whence comes salvation, but from righteousness? But if the children of God have no other way of obtaining the <hi type="italic">knowledge of salvation</hi> except <hi type="italic">through the forgiveness of sins, </hi>it follows, that righteousness must not be sought in any other quarter. Proud men attempt to forge and manufacture a righteousness out of the merits of good works. True righteousness is nothing else than the imputation of righteousness, when God, out of free grace, acquits us from guilt. Besides, it ought to be observed that Zacharias is not speaking of <hi type="italic">“</hi>strangers from the covenants of promise,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.12">Ephesians 2:12</reference>) but of the people of God. Hence it follows, that not only does the commencement of righteousness depend on the <hi type="italic">forgiveness of sins, </hi>but it is by imputation <note n="82"> <div sID="gen96064" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Imputative, ut italoquar</foreign>.” — “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par imputation, c'est a dire, d'autant que la justice de Christ laur est imputee</foreign>.” — “By imputation, that is to say, in so far as the righteousnes of Christ is imputed to them”<div eID="gen96064" type="x-p"/> </note> that believers are righteous before God to the very end: for they cannot appear before his tribunal in any other way than by betaking themselves daily to a free reconciliation.<div eID="gen96063" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.77" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96059" osisID="Luke.1.77" type="section"/>
entries.e8d4a641236f42503162ca9bff67f00d68b44357: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.78" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.1.78" sID="gen96065" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">78.</hi> <hi type="italic">Through the bowels</hi> <note n="83"> <div sID="gen96067" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par les entrailles de la misericorde, ou, par l'affection misericordieuse</foreign>.” — “By the bowels of mercy, or, by the merciful affection.”<div eID="gen96067" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">of mercy</hi> In so great a benefit Zacharias justly extols the mercy of God, and not satisfied with merely calling it the salvation which was brought by Christ, he employs more emphatic language, and says that it proceeded from the very <hi type="italic">bowels of the mercy </hi>of God. He then tells us metaphorically, that the great mercy of God has made the day to <hi type="italic">give light to those who were sitting in darkness</hi> <hi type="italic">Oriens, </hi>in the Latin version of this passage, is not a participle: for the Greek word is <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀνατολή</foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>that is, the Eastern region, as contrasted with the West. Zacharias extols the <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> of God, as manifested in dispelling the darkness of death, and restoring to the people of God the light of life. In this way, whenever our salvation is the subject, we ought to raise our minds to the contemplation of the divine mercy. There appears to be an allusion to a prediction of Malachi, in which Christ is called “the Sun of Righteousness,” and is said to “arise with healing in his wing,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.4.2">Malachi 4:2</reference>,) that is, to bring health in his rays.<div eID="gen96066" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.1.78" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96065" osisID="Luke.1.78" type="section"/>
entries.26247368377b5b1319484e9515d462c7d0a24b89:
79. That he might give light to those who were sitting in darkness As to light and darkness, there are similar modes of expression in Isaiah: such as,
“The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined,” (Isaiah 9:1;)
and in many other passages. These words show, that out of Christ there is no life-giving light in the world, but every thing is covered by the appalling darkness of death. Thus, in another passage, Isaiah testifies that this privilege belongs peculiarly to the church alone.
“Behold, the darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people: but the Lord shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen upon thee,” (Isaiah 60:2.)
But how could it be said that the Israelites, on whose hearts the Lord always shone by faith, were sitting in the shadow of death? I reply, the godly, who lived under the law were surrounded on every side by the darkness of death, and beheld at a distance, in the coming of Christ, the light that cheered and preserved them from being overwhelmed by present death. Zacharias may have had in view the wretched condition of his own age. But it is a general truth, that on all the godly, who had ever lived, or who were afterwards to live, there arose in the coming of Christ a light to impart life: for it even diffused life over the dead. To sit is of the same import as to lie:
“Estre assis emporte autant comme estre couch, ou veautre.”— “To sit is of the same import as to be lying or wallowing.”
and so Isaiah enjoins the Church, “Arise, for thy light is come,” (Isaiah 60:1.)
To guide our feet By this expression Zacharias points out, that the highest perfection of all excellence and happiness is to be found in Christ alone. The word Peace might indeed be taken in its literal sense, which would not be unsuitable: for the illumination brought by Christ tends to pacify the minds of men. But as the Hebrew word שלום, peace, denotes every kind of prosperity, Zacharias intended, I doubt not, to represent Christ as the author of perfect blessedness, that we may not seek the smallest portion of happiness elsewhere, but may rest on Christ alone, from a full conviction that in him we are entirely and completely happy. To this purpose are those words of Isaiah,
“The sun shall be no more thy light by day, neither for brightness shall the moon give light unto thee: but the Lord shall be unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory,” (Isaiah 60:19.)
But if the mere sight of his Son, while still a child, led Zacharias to discourse in so lofty a strain respecting the grace and power of Christ, before he was born, are not they so much the more ungrateful, who, now that Christ has died, and risen, and ascended to heaven, and sat down at his Father’s right hand, speak disrespectfully of him and of his power, to which the Holy Spirit bore testimony, while he was still in his mother’s womb? We must bear in mind what I have already mentioned, that Zacharias spake not from himself, but that the Spirit of God directed his tongue.
And the child grew This is added by Luke for continuing the thread of the history. First, he mentions that John became strong in spirit: which implies that the great and uncommon excellence of the child gave proof that there dwelt in him a Heavenly Spirit. Next, he tells us, that John remained unknown in the deserts till the day of his showing, that is, till the day on which the Lord had pur-posed to bring him into public view. Hence we conclude, that John, though he was fully aware of his calling, made no advances before the appointed time, but awaited the call of God.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="1" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. I.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 FOr as much as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 2.3. 1 Joh. 1.1.</ns0:note> Even as they delivered them unto us, which <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 15.27.</ns0:note> from the beginning were eye-witnesses, and ministers of the word.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 1.1.</ns0:note> excellent Theophi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lus.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 That thou mightest know the certainty of those things wherein thou hast been instructed.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Lukes</ns0:hi> Evangelical History hath this pecular to it self, That whereas the Histories of the other <ns0:hi>Evangelists</ns0:hi> are written to the whole World, having no particular Inscription, or Dedication. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> dedicates his to a particular Person, named <ns0:hi>Theophilus</ns0:hi>; for tho that Name signifyeth, <ns0:hi>one that loveth God,</ns0:hi> yet I cannot think it is to be taken here <ns0:hi>Appellatively,</ns0:hi> it being commonly u<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed as a <ns0:hi>Proper Name.</ns0:hi> Parents in former Ages giving Children Names generally either expressive of their Childrens Duty to God (that by their Names they might be put in mind of it) or Expressive, of Gods Mercy to themselves in giving them such Children. The Evangelist here suggesteth, <ns0:hi>That many had ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken in Hand,</ns0:hi> orderly to Write an account, of <ns0:hi>the things which were certainly believed amongst the Iews</ns0:hi>; some think that <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> here reflecteth upon some, that even so early had given false ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />counts of our Saviours History; for there were several pretended Gospels wrote, called, The <ns0:hi>Gospel</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Nazareans,</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Thomas, Mathias, Nicodemus,</ns0:hi> and many others which the Church soon saw cause to reject. But others think that <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> doth not at all reflect, and possibly those Figments were not so early; but <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> observing that many did Write this famous History, and some possibly, for want of due information, not so exactly, as they might, yet as they were <ns0:hi>delivered to them, from such as from the beginning were Eye-Witnesses, and Ministers of the Word,</ns0:hi> but possibly might not be able so exactly to inform them or the Writers not so able duly to digest them (for most think <ns0:hi>Matthew, Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> wrote after.) Or possibly, because there being then no Printing, but all in <ns0:hi>Manuscripts,</ns0:hi> because he thought, his Friend <ns0:hi>Theophilus</ns0:hi> (to whom he knew such an History would be grateful) might not have come to the sight of those Manuscripts, he undertakes <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> not without the direction of the Holy Spirit as appeared afterward) to Compile an Histo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry of these things, to which he was either incouraged by the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ample of others, or recited by the Mistakes of those who had done it <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> having the advantage <ns0:hi>perfectly to understand all things <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the first.</ns0:hi> most think that this advantage arose not from his Personal Knowledge. but his Converse with the Apostles and other Ministers of Christ; for he saith no more, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. then <ns0:hi>even at the delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were Eye-Witnesses, and Ministers of the Word.</ns0:hi> By which it <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to be hinted to us, that he was no <ns0:hi>Eye-Witness, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Minister of the Word.</ns0:hi> To understand by the <ns0:hi>Word</ns0:hi> in that <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> Christ (whom <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> indeed so calleth, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.1.) seemeth to me too hard, considering <ns0:hi>the Word</ns0:hi> in the E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vangelists, doth ordinarily signify the Gospel, and no where <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> but in <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.1.2. <ns0:hi>&c. That thou mightest know the certainty of th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>se things wherein thou hast been instructed.</ns0:hi> That this, by the Relation of others. Before I pass this Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />face, I shall make some Observations upon it. 1. <ns0:hi>That even from the beginning there were some Cheats, in reporting mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters of Fact concerning the Church,</ns0:hi> whether <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> intended to reflect on them, or no, if we may believe any thing of <ns0:hi>Ecclesi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />astical</ns0:hi> History, there were some false <ns0:hi>Gospels</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and before the time of the <ns0:hi>Gospel</ns0:hi> there were <ns0:hi>Apocryphal Writings</ns0:hi> relating to the History of the Old Testament, No Writings but the Scriptures deserve our Faith, (otherwise then they agree with them) in things of which they give us an account. 2. In <ns0:hi>Lukes time the History of the Gospel was most surely believed,</ns0:hi> as being delivered from Eye-Witnesses. 3. <ns0:hi>Men ought to have perfect understanding of matters of Fact<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> before they Write them.</ns0:hi> Whoso Writes a History upon incertainty, imposeth up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on all future Ages. 4. <ns0:hi>A Knowledge of Certainties, is, what all good Men ought to aim at in Writing, and Reading.</ns0:hi> It is a mean Soul that can feed upon an incertainty, and they are as mean that spend their time in catoring such Food for rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonable Souls. Mens understandings are given them for No<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bler uses, than to gain the Notion of a False-hood, and they are low-born-Souls that can spend their precious Hours in such Coo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kery, let the Sauce with which they serve it up be never so Artificial.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:292" />5 There was in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 2.1.</ns0:note> the days of Herod the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chr. 24.10.</ns0:note> of the course of Abia, and his wife <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> of the daughters of Aaron, and her name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Elizabeth.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Holy Ghost for infinitely wise Reasons, giveth us here an account both of the time when <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Baptist</ns0:hi> was born, and also of his Parentage. <ns0:hi>It was</ns0:hi> in the time of <ns0:hi>Herod the King</ns0:hi> of Judea, that is, <ns0:hi>he</ns0:hi> who was the Son of <ns0:hi>Antipater</ns0:hi> (not <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Tetrarch of Galilee,</ns0:hi> of whom you read, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 3.1. who put <ns0:hi>Iohn Baptist</ns0:hi> to Death (that was thirty one or thirty two years after this, he is usually called <ns0:hi>Herod the great,</ns0:hi> who fought his way to the Government of the Jews (under the <ns0:hi>Ro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mans</ns0:hi>) and came to his Throne by the Slaughter of the <ns0:hi>Iewish San<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>edrim,</ns0:hi> by which means he also extinguished all the <ns0:hi>Govern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment,</ns0:hi> which till his time held in the <ns0:hi>Tribe</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> tho not in a single Person, (for that was destroyed in <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> soon after the time of <ns0:hi>Iudas Maccabeus</ns0:hi>) yet in a Select Number out of that Royal Tribe. So that in this <ns0:hi>Herods</ns0:hi> time the Prophecy of dy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:hi>Iacob, Gen.</ns0:hi> 49.10. was fulfilled. <ns0:hi>The Scepter,</ns0:hi> that is, the Government <ns0:hi>departed from</ns0:hi> Juda, <ns0:hi>and the Lawgiver from his Feet,</ns0:hi> which was a certain Sign (in order to the fulfilling of that <ns0:hi>Prophecy</ns0:hi>) that <ns0:hi>Shilob,</ns0:hi> that is, the <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi> was coming. This for the time. <ns0:hi>A certain Priest, named</ns0:hi> Zacharias, some will have him to have been the <ns0:hi>High Priest,</ns0:hi> or his <ns0:hi>Deputy,</ns0:hi> but that cannot be, for the <ns0:hi>High Priest</ns0:hi> was but one, and so not within the Courses of the Priest, but of the Eldest Family from <ns0:hi>Aaron</ns0:hi>; and tho it be said <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. that his <ns0:hi>Lot was to Burn Incense,</ns0:hi> yet it must not be understood of the <ns0:hi>Incense</ns0:hi> mentioned, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 16.12. to be Burned upon the yearly <ns0:hi>Day of Exp<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ation,</ns0:hi> (which indeed none but the High Priest might do,) but of the daily Incense mentioned in the Law, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30.6, 7, 8. which any of the Priests did in their Courses. This <ns0:hi>Zacharias</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>of the</ns0:hi> Course of <ns0:hi>Abia.</ns0:hi> The Eldest Son of <ns0:hi>Aaron</ns0:hi> was always the <ns0:hi>High Priest,</ns0:hi> his other Sons were Priests; in a long Course of time, their De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scendants so Multiplyed, that they were too many all at the same time to Minister in the Temple. <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> therefore divided them into Courses, each Course waited their Month, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 24.5, 6. there is an account of the Distribution of the Priests into twenty four Courses. In <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> time the Eighth Course, was the Course of <ns0:hi>Abia,</ns0:hi> it appeareth by <ns0:hi>Nehemiah</ns0:hi> 124, 17. That after the Captivity they kept the Denominations of these Courses, but it is probable the order of them was altered. We Read of <ns0:hi>Abiah,</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Nehem.</ns0:hi> 12. but whether his was then, or at this time when <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> Wrote his Gospel, the <ns0:hi>Eighth Course</ns0:hi> I cannot tell. It is enough for us, that <ns0:hi>Zachariah</ns0:hi> was one of the ordinary Priests of the <ns0:hi>Course of Abia.</ns0:hi> Whose Office it was to serve in the Temple in his Course (which was the Course of such as derived from the <ns0:hi>Abia,</ns0:hi> mentioned in 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 24.5, 6.) <ns0:hi>And his Wife was of the Daughters of</ns0:hi> Aaron, <ns0:hi>and her Name was</ns0:hi> Elizabeth. This is added not to signify <ns0:hi>Zacharias</ns0:hi> his obedience to the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Law, which obliged the Priests to marry within their own Tribes, for the reason of that Law, being only to prevent the Confusion of the Inheritances, which fell by Lot to the several Tribes, and by the Will of God were to be so kept distinct, th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Tribes of <ns0:hi>Levi</ns0:hi> having no such Inheritance, might intermix with any other Tribe, and did so, the <ns0:hi>High Priest</ns0:hi> was only ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liged to Marry some of his own people, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 21.14. and <ns0:hi>Iehojada,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 11.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>2. Married one of the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iuda,</ns0:hi> but it is add<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to shew the Honourableness of <ns0:hi>Elizabeths</ns0:hi> Stock. <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> were the two first Governours of the <ns0:hi>Israelites. Eliza<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />beth</ns0:hi> was not only of the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Levi,</ns0:hi> but descended from <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> whom God made the Noblest Family of the <ns0:hi>Levites.</ns0:hi> Her Name was <ns0:hi>Elizabeth.</ns0:hi> It is an <ns0:hi>Hebrew Name, Exod.</ns0:hi> 6 23. and (as you may see there) was the very Name of <ns0:hi>Aarons</ns0:hi> Wife the <ns0:hi>Daughter of Aminadab,</ns0:hi> and Sister of <ns0:hi>Naashon.</ns0:hi> As it may be variously Written it signifyeth, <ns0:hi>The Rest,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>the Oath,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>the Rod of my God.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord, blameless.<ns0:note place="bottom">That they were not Righteous by a perfect Legal Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness, being not guilty of any Sin is certain, for so there is <ns0:hi>none Righteous, no not one,</ns0:hi> but so Righteous, as that God ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepted them, and looked upon them as Righteous, as <ns0:hi>Abraham believed,</ns0:hi> and it <ns0:hi>was imputed to him for Righteousness,</ns0:hi> tho he Sinned in the denyal of his Wife, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> or as it is said of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 15.5. <ns0:hi>He did that which was Right in the Eyes of the Lord, and turned not aside from any thing which he com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded him all the Days of his Life, save only in the matter of Vriah.</ns0:hi> They <ns0:hi>also Walked in all the Commandments and Ordinances of the Lord, Blameless.</ns0:hi> A Man's Blameless Conver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sation before the World, is a piece of his righteousness, but will not make up alone such a Righteousness, as will testify his Ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceptation with God, or <ns0:hi>Righteousness</ns0:hi> before him; he must in the first place, <ns0:hi>Walk in the Commandments, and in the Ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nances of God.</ns0:hi> There is a Duty towards God, as well as toward Men: and that Duty lies in the keeping <ns0:hi>his Commandments,</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Ordinances</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>fear of the Lord,</ns0:hi> must not be taught us by the <ns0:hi>Precepts of Men.</ns0:hi> Yea, and in all the <ns0:hi>Ordinances</ns0:hi> of God ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving a respect to all Gods Commandments, and making this his constant Course and Practice not doing it by fits, he must also be <ns0:hi>blamless</ns0:hi> towards Men. Here is a true Pattern of what a Mar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ried Couple should be, especially where the Husband waits at the Altar, and is imployed in the holy things of God. A <ns0:hi>Bishop</ns0:hi> must be blameless, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.2. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8. A <ns0:hi>Deacon Grave,</ns0:hi> not dou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Tongued, not given to much Wine, not greedy of filthy Lu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cre—<ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10. <ns0:hi>Blameless</ns0:hi>; and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. <ns0:hi>Even so must their Wives be Grave, not Slanderers, Sober,</ns0:hi> &c. such were <ns0:hi>Zacharias</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Elizabeth.</ns0:hi> Such ought all Ministers of the Gospel, and their Wives to be.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And they had no child, because that Elizabeth was barren, and they both were <ns0:hi>now</ns0:hi> well stricken in years.<ns0:note place="bottom">Amongst all Earthly Blessings, there is nothing we more de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire then Children, in whom we have a kind of Perpetuity, living in our Species and in our Posterity, when we are dead in Nature; but as God for our Tryal, doth often deny us other good things which are the great objects of our desires, so he doth often deny his own People this great Blessing. Sometimes he withholdeth it a long time from those to whom he at length giveth it. Bar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />renness in <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> was a Reproach. See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25. and 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1.6. There was a promise to <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> of a <ns0:hi>plentiful Seed,</ns0:hi> hence a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst the Jews, she that was Barren hardly thought her self, or was judged by others a Genuine Daughter of <ns0:hi>Abraham.</ns0:hi> Both <ns0:hi>Zachariah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Elizabeth,</ns0:hi> were now well stricken in Years God chuseth this Woman naturally Barren, and now Aged, also, to be the Mother of <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist,</ns0:hi> therein working a double Miracle; and it is observable in Holy Writ, that when God deny<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to any Women Children for some long time, and then open<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed their Wombs, they were the Mothers of some Eminent Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons, whom God made great use of. Thus it was with <ns0:hi>Sarah, Rachel,</ns0:hi> the Wife of <ns0:hi>Manoah, Hannah,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. and this <ns0:hi>Elizabeth.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And it came to pass, that while he executed the priests office before God in the order of his course,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 According to the custom of the priests office, his lot was to <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 30.7. Lev. 16.17.</ns0:note> burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Priests were Multiplyed to an exceeding Number, we find an account of more then 4000 upon the return out of the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon, Ezra</ns0:hi> 3.36, 37, 38, 39. they were doubt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less afterward multiplyed to a far greater number, <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> tells us there were a thousand in a Course; whether they held to twen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty four Courses as in <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> time or no I cannot tell. There were several parts of the <ns0:hi>Priestly Office,</ns0:hi> which it seemeth by this Text, the Priests of the Course that Ministred, divided amongst themselves by a Lot, one part of their Work was to <ns0:hi>Burn In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cense Morning and Evening.</ns0:hi> It seems this was that part of the Priestly Office, which <ns0:hi>Zacharias</ns0:hi> was by Lot to Exercise.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And the whole multitude of the people were praying without, at the time of incense <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 30.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Levit. 16.17.</ns0:note>
                  <ns0:note place="bottom">We are told, that the order of the Jewish daily Service was this. Twice in the Day the Priests. (whose Course it was to Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nister, or such of them whose Lot it was) went into the Holy Place to Burn Incense according to the Law, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30.7. when they went in A <ns0:hi>Bell Rung</ns0:hi> to give notice, that it was the hour of <ns0:hi>Prayer</ns0:hi>; there were constantly there, 1. <ns0:hi>The rest of the Priests of the same Course.</ns0:hi> 2. The <ns0:hi>Levites.</ns0:hi> 3. Their <ns0:hi>Stationary men, who re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />presented the whole Congregation,</ns0:hi> and laid their Hands upon the Beast slain. 4. So many more of the People as would Volunta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rily come, and it was very ordinary for many to go (thus we read <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 31. of <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> going into the Temple at the <ns0:hi>Hour of Prayer</ns0:hi>) these made the Multitude of whom it is said, that while the Priest was <ns0:hi>Burning Incense,</ns0:hi> they were <ns0:hi>without,</ns0:hi> not without the Temple, but in the <ns0:hi>Court of Israel,</ns0:hi> without the <ns0:hi>Holy Place,</ns0:hi> in which the Priests was Burning Incense. <ns0:hi>Praying</ns0:hi> so they used to do privately by themselves. There is a Text in <ns0:hi>Ecclesiasticus, Ch.</ns0:hi> 50.15. which (tho it be not Canonical Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, yet as Credible as any other Civil History, and will much help to make the <ns0:hi>Readers</ns0:hi> understand the order of the Jewish Service, and what this Text saith.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:292" />11 And there appeared unto him an angel of the Lord, standing on the right side of the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 30.1.</ns0:note> altar of in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cense.<ns0:note place="bottom">Tho we Translate it <ns0:hi>appeared,</ns0:hi> yet in the Greek it is, there <ns0:hi>was seen of him.</ns0:hi> An <ns0:hi>Angel</ns0:hi> indeed was there, whether the Angel <ns0:hi>Gabriel</ns0:hi> or no, or in what form he appeared, it is not said. It is by some observed, That untill the <ns0:hi>Vrim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Thummim</ns0:hi> ceased. No Angel appeared to any Priest Executing his Office, after this it is observed by others, that most appearances of <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> to the Priests were, when they were imployed in their Service in the Temple.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And when Zacharias saw <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> he was troubled, and fear fell upon him.<ns0:note place="bottom">We are naturally affrighted, at sudden, and unusual things, but especially at any Divine appearances, whether God himself takes a shape, or Authorizeth an <ns0:hi>Angel</ns0:hi> to do it. So was <ns0:hi>Dani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />el, Ch.</ns0:hi> 10.7, 8. and <ns0:hi>Manoah</ns0:hi> and his Wife, <ns0:hi>Iud.</ns0:hi> 13.20. and <ns0:hi>Paul, Acts</ns0:hi> 9. for tho God doth not make these appearances to affright us, yet such is the Imbecillity of our Natures, that we cannot but be shy at them, and start from them, and it is but rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonable, that God should by this means, both declare his own Glory<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and Majesty, and also humble his Poor Creatures, and make them more Impre<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sive, and Receptive of his Divine <ns0:hi>Reve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lations.</ns0:hi> It is reasonable God should keep and declare his Maje<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sty, tho we keep and declare our Infirmity.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 But the angel said unto him, Fear not, Zacha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rias, for thy prayer is heard, and thy wife Elizabeth shall bear thee a son, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 60.63.</ns0:note> thou shalt call his name John.<ns0:note place="bottom">Altho the great God useth so to shew himself to the best of his own People, as to imprint upon them a sacred aw of his Majesty, yet he never suffereth the Souls of his People to sink under those apprehensions. The fir<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> t Words, the <ns0:hi>Angel</ns0:hi> saith to <ns0:hi>Zacharias,</ns0:hi> are, <ns0:hi>Fear not Zacharias.</ns0:hi> I am no bad Messenger to thee, but a good Messenger from God, to tell thee, <ns0:hi>Thy Prayer is heard.</ns0:hi> This is good news to any Soul. But of what Prayer the <ns0:hi>Angel</ns0:hi> here speaketh, is a little further question, for it follows, <ns0:hi>And thy Wife</ns0:hi> Eliz<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>beth <ns0:hi>shall bear thee a Son.</ns0:hi> It is believed that the Priest while he Burned Incense, did offer up Prayers, but that he had now offered Prayers to God for issue, is not so probable, consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dering that both he and <ns0:hi>Elizabeth</ns0:hi> were well stricken in years, and probably past Children. Some therefore think that those Words. <ns0:hi>And thy Wife</ns0:hi> Elizabeth, &c. are given him only as a Sign, that his Prayers were heard. And added to signify that as a further Mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy to him than what he asked, <ns0:hi>Elizabeth</ns0:hi> should conceive. Nor do I see any reason why we should restrain the <ns0:hi>Prayer</ns0:hi> mentio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned to the Prayer he had now made, and not expound it of those many Prayers which <ns0:hi>Zacharias</ns0:hi> had before made, which tho God had delay'd to Answer, yet the Angel assures him, should now be answered with Relation to issue, <ns0:hi>And thou shalt call his Name</ns0:hi> John, which is the same with <ns0:hi>Iohanan</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> and signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies <ns0:hi>Gracious.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Angel</ns0:hi> directed <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> to call Christs Name <ns0:hi>Iesus, Because he was to save his People from their Sins,</ns0:hi> and he directeth <ns0:hi>Zachariah</ns0:hi> to call his Sons Name <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> because he was to open the Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Grace,</ns0:hi> and to Preach the <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Gospel,</ns0:hi> through Jesus Christ.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>and he shall be to thee joy and glad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> And thou shalt have joy and gladness, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 58.</ns0:note> many shall rejoyce at his birth.<ns0:note place="bottom">None ought to have so mean thoughts of these Words of the <ns0:hi>Angel,</ns0:hi> as to think that they are only expressive of that Affecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, which commonly discovereth it self in us, when God giveth us Sons, especially after a long Barrenness, but of a further joy and gladness, his Parents should have upon a spiritual account afterwards exprest. <ns0:hi>Many shall rejoyce at his Birth, Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.36. they rejoyced <ns0:hi>in his light,</ns0:hi> the glad Tidnigs of the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> being come into the World, which he brought. The <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> think they have a ground here for their Holy-day, they keep to his Honour, and their Apish Carnal rejoycing, which certainly, was not so valuable a thing, as for an Angel to foretel. The Angel speaks of the great Acceptation with the People, (many of them) which <ns0:hi>Iohns Doctrine</ns0:hi> should have, so that as our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our saith, <ns0:hi>From his Days the Kingdom of Heaven suffered Violence, and the Violent did take it by force.</ns0:hi> But he further openeth his meaning, in the following Verses.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 For he shall be great in the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ight of the Lord, and shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he shall be filled with the holy Ghost,<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 1.5. Gal. 1.15.</ns0:note> even from his mothers womb.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Malachy 4.</ns0:note> And many of the children of Israel shall he turn to the Lord their God.<ns0:note place="bottom">We have a natural Ambition to be <ns0:hi>great,</ns0:hi> but it is only to be great in the sight of Men, thence one Man coveteth Riches, ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Honours, and Reputation, but the true greatness is to be <ns0:hi>great in the sight of the Lord,</ns0:hi> who doth certainly judge with the truest and most infallible Judgment. In Gods sight he is a <ns0:hi>great Man,</ns0:hi> of whom God maketh a great use, especially in turning many Souls to himself. Consider <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> separately from his Work, and the Concurrence of God with his Work, he was a <ns0:hi>very little Man,</ns0:hi> and so looked upon, by the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rulers,</ns0:hi> who would not <ns0:hi>believe in him.</ns0:hi> His Father was an ordinary, Priest. For Titles and Dignities, he had none, <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist</ns0:hi> was his highest Title. For his Clothing, he was not Clothed in <ns0:hi>soft Ray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment</ns0:hi> (as <ns0:hi>Princes Chaplains</ns0:hi>) he was Clothed with a <ns0:hi>Skin,</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>Camels Hair,</ns0:hi> and had a <ns0:hi>Leathern Girdle about his Loyns,</ns0:hi> yet Christ saith of him, <ns0:hi>Among those that were born of Women, there had not risen a greater than</ns0:hi> John <ns0:hi>the Baptist,</ns0:hi> he had no Palace, no Stately Habitation, he lived mostly in desert Places little Inhabited. Nature was his Cook, that provided him <ns0:hi>Lo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />custs</ns0:hi> and wild Honey. Where was his greatness, but in this? He was a great, and faithful Preacher of the Gospel; and God Blessed his Labours to convert Souls. They are little Men, that do little of the Work, for which God hath sent them into the World, and do little good in their Generation. <ns0:hi>He shall drink neither Wine nor strong Drink</ns0:hi> by strong Drink is meant any <ns0:hi>Drink</ns0:hi> which ordinarily intoxicateth. This was the <ns0:hi>Law of the Nazarites, Num.</ns0:hi> 6.3. It was forbidden the Priests during the time of their Ministration upon pain of death, <ns0:hi>Le<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vit.</ns0:hi> 10.9. No lovers of <ns0:hi>Wine</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>strong Drink</ns0:hi> can be great Men in the sight of God. The Minister of the Gospel must not be one <ns0:hi>given to Wine,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.3. <ns0:hi>Titus</ns0:hi> 1.7. <ns0:hi>And he shall be fil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led with the Holy Ghost, even from his Mothers Womb.</ns0:hi> This is true, both as to <ns0:hi>Prophecy</ns0:hi> (which is an extraordinary Gift of the Holy Ghost) and also of the Holy Ghost considered as a <ns0:hi>San<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctifying Spirit<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> renewing the Heart. <ns0:hi>For many of the Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of</ns0:hi> Israel <ns0:hi>shall he turn to the Lord their God.</ns0:hi> Then it seems there is another Conversion besides the Conversion of Men from <ns0:hi>Paganisme. Iohn</ns0:hi> (with the assistance of the Holy Ghost) was an Instrument to turn <ns0:hi>many</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> who already Ver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bally owned the true God, but were Drencht in Errors and Su<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perstitions, and loosness of Life, to the Lord their God, by Repen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance, and this he did by Preaching both Law and Gospel to them. This made him a great Man, for <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 12.3. <ns0:hi>They that turn many to Righteousness, shall shine as the Stars for ever and ever.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And he shall go before him in the spirit and po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wer of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Or by, or in.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> to the wisdom of the just, to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.<ns0:note place="bottom">God was last spoken of, he must therefore be the <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />oned here, before whom <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist</ns0:hi> was to go, according to the Prophecy, <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 4.5, 6. from whence is an evident proof, that Christ was the Lord our God, before whom <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Bap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tist</ns0:hi> came, in the <ns0:hi>Spirit and Power of</ns0:hi> Elias, and therefore he is called <ns0:hi>Elias, Mal.</ns0:hi> 4, 5. as expounded by Christ, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.14. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 9.11. The Jews not understanding this, keeps them in a vain expectation of a <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> to this Day, and of a Personal coming of <ns0:hi>Elias</ns0:hi> before him; it is the observation of some learned Men, that where the word <ns0:hi>Power</ns0:hi> is added to the <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> or holy Ghost, it signifies a more than ordinary measure, and Influence of the Spirit as in this <ns0:hi>Chap. v.</ns0:hi> 35. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 10.38. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.4. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.5. But I rather think, that by that Phrase, <ns0:hi>In the Spirit and Power</ns0:hi> here is meant, with the same Zeal and frame of Spirit that <ns0:hi>Elijah</ns0:hi> had; we have before in our Notes upon <ns0:hi>Mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thew,</ns0:hi> shewed in how many things <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist</ns0:hi> was like <ns0:hi>Elijah,</ns0:hi> to say nothing of his Habit, and the Severity of his Life, in respect of the most corrupt time, wherein they both lived, their faithfulness in their Ministry, their Warmth and Zeal in their Work, their boldness not fearing to reprove Princes for their Er<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rors, <ns0:hi>&c. to turn the Hearts of the Fathers to the Children. Malachy</ns0:hi> addeth, and the <ns0:hi>Hearts of the Children to the Parents,</ns0:hi> instead of which <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> hath, and the <ns0:hi>disobedient to the Wisdom of the just,</ns0:hi> that is, to bring both <ns0:hi>Young</ns0:hi> and Old to Repentance. The Hearts of the <ns0:hi>Fathers</ns0:hi> amongst the Jews to the Doctrine of Christ, and his Apostles their Children, and the Hearts of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> which with respect to <ns0:hi>Abraham, Isaac</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> are Children, to the Doctrine which they imbraced, and the ways of God wherein those just Men walked, which is the Doctrine of Wisdom. To reconcile many amongst the Jews to that which some of them own and profess, tho others of them are yet Aposta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tized, and yet led away, with the Superstitions of these Degene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rate, and Corrupt times. <ns0:hi>To make ready a People prepared for the Lord,</ns0:hi> to acquaint this part of the World with the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> and to prepare them for receiving him and his Doctrine, which is presently to be revealed by himself, taking off Peoples Prejudices, and discovering and commending Christ to them. Or by bringing Men to a true Repentance for their Sins, and a Sense of them, till which they cannot believe to prepare them for a more Internal Reception of the Lord Jesus Christ. For <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> is said to have Preached the Doctrine of <ns0:hi>Repentance for the Remission of Sins,</ns0:hi> and to have Preached, saying, <ns0:hi>Repent</ns0:hi> for the Kingdom of Heaven is at Hand. Also defaming the Pharisees who were the great E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nemies of Christ, by detecting to the People their Hypocrisy. Thus he <ns0:hi>made ready a People prepared for the Lord.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:293" />18 And Zacharias said unto the angel, <ns0:note place="margin">Gen. 17.17.</ns0:note> Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife well stricken in years.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Words are much the same with those of <ns0:hi>Abraham Gen.</ns0:hi> 15.8. <ns0:hi>whereby shall I know I shall inherit it,</ns0:hi> viz. the <ns0:hi>Land of Caanan?</ns0:hi> And <ns0:hi>Mary v.</ns0:hi> 34. of this Chapter, when the same Angel had told her she should have a Child, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 31. saith, <ns0:hi>How shall this be seeing I know not a Man? Gideon</ns0:hi> also asked a Sign <ns0:hi>Iud.</ns0:hi> 6.17. To our appearance and Judgment there seemeth no great difference betwixt these, and <ns0:hi>Zachariah</ns0:hi> in this place asking a Sign. Only <ns0:hi>Zachariah</ns0:hi> here opposeth his own <ns0:hi>sense</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>reason,</ns0:hi> to the Words of the Angel, yet we shall hear a different issue of this Question, or answer to it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And the angel answering, said unto him, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God: and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formed, because thou believest not my words, which shall be fulfilled in their season.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is by some observed, That before the <ns0:hi>Captivity of Babylon</ns0:hi> we read of no name of any <ns0:hi>Angel,</ns0:hi> who have no names as we have, but assume names to declare the nature of their ministration, and that <ns0:hi>Gabriel</ns0:hi> signifieth the <ns0:hi>Power,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>strength of God,</ns0:hi> because the declaring of the Gospel which the Apostle declares <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.16. <ns0:hi>The Power of God to Salvation,</ns0:hi> seemeth to have been his pecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liar Ministration. We Read of this <ns0:hi>Gabriel, Dan.</ns0:hi> 8.16. and 9.21. where we find him foretelling the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> and the working of Mans Redemption: to which Prophec<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>es he doubtless refers <ns0:hi>Zacharia</ns0:hi> in saying I <ns0:hi>am Gabriel.</ns0:hi> We again shall meet with him, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 26, 27. <ns0:hi>Six <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> after this, appearing to the <ns0:hi>Virgin Mary,</ns0:hi> and telling her she should bring forth the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> he addeth, <ns0:hi>that stand in the presence of God,</ns0:hi> as the good <ns0:hi>An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gels</ns0:hi> always behold the <ns0:hi>Presence of our Heavenly Father</ns0:hi> (as our Saviour tells us) and are ready to be sent about his Messages, (whence is the Name of <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi>) they are called <ns0:hi>Gods Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters, Psal.</ns0:hi> 103.21. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 104.4. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> am sent to <ns0:hi>speak unto thee, and to show thee glad tidings.</ns0:hi> God sent me on purpose to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clare this thing to thee. Which <ns0:hi>Zachariah</ns0:hi> might have known by the time and place, when he appeared, at the time of <ns0:hi>Prayer,</ns0:hi> at the Altar in the holy Place, where the Evil Angels used not to shew themselves. And <ns0:hi>behold thou shalt be Dumb, and not a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to speak until the Day that these things shall be performed.</ns0:hi> Divines have perplexed themselves, to give a just account of this signal Punishment of so good a Man. Whether they have said e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nough to satisfaction I cannot tell. <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> upon the same Q<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tion, was gratifyed with a Sign, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15.9.10. so was <ns0:hi>Gideon, Iud.</ns0:hi> 6.17. where there is no difference in the <ns0:hi>Words,</ns0:hi> or in a <ns0:hi>Fact,</ns0:hi> there may be a great difference in the Heart, and its inward <ns0:hi>Habit</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Motions,</ns0:hi> from which those Words proceed, and we must allow God to see that, better then we can discern it by the Words. Before <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> time, we read of no such Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perience of Gods power in such Cases, neither do we find that <ns0:hi>A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />braham</ns0:hi> desired a Sign as to this, that God would give him a Child, but only as to the Lords giving his Posterity <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi> Besides, that it is said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. <ns0:hi>He believed, and it was counted to him for Righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness,</ns0:hi> and the Apostle extolleth his Faith, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4.19. <ns0:hi>Being not weak in the Faith, he considered not his own Body now dead, when he was above a hundred years old, nor the deadness of</ns0:hi> Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rahs <ns0:hi>Womb, he staggered not at the promise through unbelief, but was strong in Faith, giving Glory to God, being fully per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suaded that what he had promised, he was able to perform.</ns0:hi> So as he asked not a Sign for the begetting of a Faith in him, he be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieved the Lord without a sight, only, fearing his own Heart, he asked a Sign for the further Increase and Confirmation of his Faith. Besides, <ns0:hi>Zachariahs</ns0:hi> punishment was <ns0:hi>Gentle,</ns0:hi> and of that Nature that it also carried with it an Answer to his desire. It was only the Privation of Speech, until the Words of the Angel should be fulfilled. <ns0:hi>Because thou believedst not my Words.</ns0:hi> The Words of God by his Messengers are to be believed, and the not believing their Words, which they speak truly from him, and as so sent, is a Sin God will severely punish. It is all one, not to believe God, as not to believe those whom he sends, speaking what he bids them. <ns0:hi>Which shall be fulfilled in their Season.</ns0:hi> The Unbelief of Men shall not make the Word, and promise of God of no effect. But Gods promises have their Seasons, before which we must not expect the Accomplishment of them. <ns0:hi>Hab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />akkuk</ns0:hi> 2.3.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And the people waited for Zacharias, and marvelled that he tarried so long in the temple.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And when he came out, he could not speak unto them, and they perceived that he had seen a vision in the temple, for he beckned unto them, and remained speechless.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And it came to pass, that as soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished, he departed to his own house.<ns0:note place="bottom">While the Priest was in the holy Place, the People were in tha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>rt of the Temple called the <ns0:hi>Court of Israel,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Court of the Pe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ple,</ns0:hi> praying, when he had done, he came out, and blessed them according to the Law, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 6.23, 24. where is the form of Blessing, which he used, for this, the People wait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed before they went home. Whether the Angels Discourse with <ns0:hi>Zacharias</ns0:hi> was longer, or his Amazement at the Vision made him stay longer then the Priest was wont to stay, it is uncertain; but so he did, and when he came out, he was not able to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nounce the Blessing, nor to speak at all, only he beckneth to them, by which the People judged, that he had seen some Visi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on. Yet <ns0:hi>Dumbness</ns0:hi> being none of those bodily defects, for which by the Law they were to be removed from the Priests Office, nor having any great Work in which he used his Tongue during his Ministration, which was more the work of the Hands, he accom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plished the Days he was to Minister, and <ns0:hi>then departed to his own House,</ns0:hi> for in the Days of their Ministration they had their Lodgings in Buildings appertaining to the Temple.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And after those days his wife Elizabeth con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceived, and hid her self five months, saying,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Thus hath the Lord dealt with me, in the days wherein he looked on me, to <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 30.23. Isa. 4.1.</ns0:note> take away my reproach among men.<ns0:note place="bottom">How long after those Days the Scripture saith not, but it is probable it was soon after, as in the Case of <ns0:hi>Abraham.</ns0:hi> And in the Case of <ns0:hi>Manoahs</ns0:hi> Wife, <ns0:hi>Iud.</ns0:hi> 13.3. who conceived present<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly after the Revelation, <ns0:hi>and hid her self under ground,</ns0:hi> not that she hid her self from seeing any Person, but she concealed from those whom she saw, the hopes that she had of her being with Child, and perhaps what her Husband had let her know by Wri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting of the <ns0:hi>Revelation</ns0:hi> he had from the <ns0:hi>Angel,</ns0:hi> not that she her self doubted the thing, that were unreasonable to presume<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> after the seeing of her Husband made Dumb for a Sign of it, and her next Word will let us know the contrary, but to avoid the Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course of People upon so unusual a thing, who might possibly think her too Vain in speaking of a thing so improbable, and unlikely as this was. In the mean time she did not Conceal her self from God, but said, <ns0:hi>Thus hath the Lord dealt with me,</ns0:hi> A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scribing it all to the Power of God, who keepeth the Key of the Womb in his Hand, and maketh the Fruit of it his Reward, <ns0:hi>In the Days wherein he looked upon me,</ns0:hi> it is the same with, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 48. <ns0:hi>he hath regarded the low Estate of his Hand-maid.</ns0:hi> The Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour of God to his Creatures is oft expressed under this Notion, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 25.18. and 84.9. and 119.132. To <ns0:hi>take away my Reproach amongst Men.</ns0:hi> Barrenness is no more then a Reproach amongst Men, it was more especially a Reproach to <ns0:hi>Iewish Wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men,</ns0:hi> not only in regard of the Expectation of being the Mother of the <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi> (for none could expect that but a <ns0:hi>Virgin, Isaiah</ns0:hi> 7.14. and she of <ns0:hi>the Tribe of</ns0:hi> Judah, to which the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> was pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mised, and one of the House of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> to whose Family he was promised as a Branch) but in regard of the special promise to <ns0:hi>A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />braham,</ns0:hi> to whom a Seed was promised, numerous as the Dust, and as the Stars, to which the <ns0:hi>Barren Woman,</ns0:hi> could contribute nothing. It is a great Mercy when God favoureth his People with any Providences, which take away <ns0:hi>their Reproach amongst Men,</ns0:hi> and a just cause for his Peoples thankful acknowledgment.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent from God, unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 To a virgin <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 1.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgins name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Mary.<ns0:note place="bottom">In the sixth Month, that is, after <ns0:hi>Elizabeths</ns0:hi> conception, thus it is Expounded afterward, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 36. The <ns0:hi>Angel Gabriel,</ns0:hi> the same <ns0:hi>Angel</ns0:hi> that had appeared in the Temple to <ns0:hi>Zacharias,</ns0:hi> who seem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth to have had a special Ministration, with reference to that part of Gods Will, which was predictive of the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> he was <ns0:hi>sent from God,</ns0:hi> (without whose command the <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> do not move) to a <ns0:hi>City of</ns0:hi> Galilee <ns0:hi>called</ns0:hi> Nazareth. There <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> lived, from thence he went, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 2.4. The Angel came to the <ns0:hi>Virgin,</ns0:hi> who is here described by her Name <ns0:hi>Mary,</ns0:hi> and her <ns0:hi>Relation,</ns0:hi> she was espoused to one <ns0:hi>Ioseph,</ns0:hi> who is said, to be of the House of <ns0:hi>David. Matthew</ns0:hi> reduceth his Genealogy to prove him to be so.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And the angel came in unto her, and said, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>God save thee, or rejoyce.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Hail thou that <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>thou that hast obtained favour.</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>thou that art freely be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ved.</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>much grace.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> art highly favoured, the Lord <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with thee, blessed <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> thou among women.<ns0:note place="bottom">Virgins betrothed, until the Consummation of their Marriage, were ordinarily kept in their Friends House, thither came this Angel, and saith, <ns0:hi>Hail thou that art highly favoured.</ns0:hi> The Word Translated <ns0:hi>Hail</ns0:hi> signifies <ns0:hi>Rejoyce thou,</ns0:hi> or is as much as <ns0:hi>God save thee.</ns0:hi> It is not the form of a Prayer (as the Papists use it) but an ordinary Salutation, as much as, <ns0:hi>God save you</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>Good-morrow</ns0:hi> is amongst us, <ns0:hi>Thou that art highly favoured,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the word comes originally from <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> which signifyeth in Scripture two things. 1. <ns0:hi>The free Love, and favour of another bestowed on any,</ns0:hi> that it is taken, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. thou hast found favour, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.6. <ns0:hi>to the Praise of the Glory of his Grace.</ns0:hi> 2. It signifies <ns0:hi>good Habits in the Soul,</ns0:hi> as 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.18. <ns0:hi>grow in Grace, Col.</ns0:hi> 3.16. <ns0:hi>Singing with Grace in your Hearts.</ns0:hi> Hence the <ns0:hi>Verb,</ns0:hi> a Participle from which the word here used is, may signify two things. Either <ns0:hi>thou hast received Grace or favour</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>rom God, or, 2. <ns0:hi>Thou that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> habits.</ns0:hi> The first seems to be its sense in this place<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> it followeth in the verse. <ns0:hi>Blessed art thou,</ns0:hi> so also it is expounded <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>thou hast found favour with God.</ns0:hi> So as the Virgin was the object of Divine Grace, as we are, and therefore not to be prayed to, as the <ns0:hi>Fountain of Grace,</ns0:hi> she her self had nothing but what she received. This whole verse seemeth to be only a <ns0:hi>Salutation,</ns0:hi> there is nothing of a Prayer in it, the Angel doth only take notice of her, as a favourite of Heaven, one dear unto his Lord, with whom God was in an especial manner, and whom God blessed above the rate of those <ns0:hi>ordinary Blessings,</ns0:hi> with which he blesseth other Women.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:293" />29 And when she saw him, she was troubled at his saying, and cast in her mind what manner of salu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion this should be.<ns0:note place="bottom">It seemeth that she did not only hear a voice, and saw an ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary appearance, but the appearance of the Angel, was attended with some manifestation of the Glory of God, which affected her and made her admire, what the meaning of this should be, that God should send an Angel to her, and with such a kind of Salu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found favour with God.<ns0:note place="bottom">This expounds those words, <ns0:hi>thou art highly favoured, v.</ns0:hi> 28. and lets her know, that he came upon no ill design unto her, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther upon any Humane errand, nor yet with any message of evil tidings from God, for she was one for whom God had a favour.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2.21.</ns0:note> shalt call his name Jesus.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest, and the Lord God <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 132.11.</ns0:note> shall give unto him the throne of his father David.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Dan. 2.44. Heb. 1.8.</ns0:note> And he shall reign over the house of Ja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cob for ever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.<ns0:note place="bottom">These three verses contain the substance of the Angels message, or errand to the Virgin, to tell her she should be the Mother of a <ns0:hi>Son.</ns0:hi> By what name she should call him, and what he should be. In telling her this, who knew her self to be a Virgin, one who had not known Man, (as she expresseth it, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 34.) he plainly mindeth her that the Prophecy <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 7.14. should be fulfilled in her. Thus far the Angels Word signify a promise. <ns0:hi>And thou shalt call his name Iesus,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Angel, Matth.</ns0:hi> 1.21. saith the same to <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> and expounds it, adding, <ns0:hi>for he shall save his People from their Sinns,</ns0:hi> and thus the Prophet expoundeth it who saith, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 7.14. his name should be called <ns0:hi>Emanuel,</ns0:hi> there were two of this name before, <ns0:hi>Ioshua</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iehoshua,</ns0:hi> both of which were great types of Christ, as being great temporal Saviours to the Israelites. The one brought them into <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi> The other led them out of <ns0:hi>Babylon, Ezra.</ns0:hi> 2.2. But this was yet a more ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellent <ns0:hi>Ioshuah,</ns0:hi> who was to save his People from their Sins. The Angel further goes on describing him, saying. <ns0:hi>He shall be great, Isaiah</ns0:hi> had said <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 9.6. His name shall be called <ns0:hi>wonderful mighty both in Words and deeds, Luke</ns0:hi> 24.19. <ns0:hi>And shall be called the Son of the Highest,</ns0:hi> that is the Son of God, who is often in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture made known by this name, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 14.19. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 92.1 <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 83.18. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 5.7. <ns0:hi>He shall be called the Son,</ns0:hi> that is, he shall <ns0:hi>be so,</ns0:hi> for this Phrase so signifieth often, <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 1.26. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.12. for he shall be <ns0:hi>known,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>declared to be so, Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.4. <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> so called him, so did the <ns0:hi>Centurion</ns0:hi> who attended his Cross, God himself called him so, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 2.7. and that in a sense, agreeing to none but him, no not to the <ns0:hi>Angels, Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.5. much less to Saints. <ns0:hi>And the Lord God shall give unto him, the throne of his Father</ns0:hi> David. Not the temporal Kingdom, but the Spiritual Kingdom over the same People over whom <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> ruled, from whom he is descended. It appeareth from many passages in the Prophets that <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> Kingdom, was a type of Christs, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7.13. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 2.6 <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 132.11. <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 9.6, 7. <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 9.11. Hence we find the name of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> given to Christ, <ns0:hi>Ieremy</ns0:hi> 30.9. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 34.23. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 37.24. <ns0:hi>Hosea</ns0:hi> 3.5. <ns0:hi>And he shall reign over the house of</ns0:hi> Jacob <ns0:hi>for ever, and of his Kingdom shall be no end. Iacob</ns0:hi> was the Father of the twelve Tribes of <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi> So as the <ns0:hi>house of Iacob,</ns0:hi> primarily signifieth the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> who were the <ns0:hi>natural Branches,</ns0:hi> in this excellent <ns0:hi>Olive.</ns0:hi> Christs Kingdom ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tended beyond the house of <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> but it began there, his Law went first out of <ns0:hi>Sion,</ns0:hi> and he was in the first place sent to the <ns0:hi>lost Sheep of Israel,</ns0:hi> he was <ns0:hi>the Minister of the Circumcision, Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.8. others were to be <ns0:hi>joyned to the house of</ns0:hi> Jacob, <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 14.1. or <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> and the house of <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> may signify the whole Church<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> all that should believe in Christ. <ns0:hi>The Rod of his strength went out of Sion, Psal.</ns0:hi> 110.2. tho his Kingdom was not con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fined to <ns0:hi>Iacob.</ns0:hi> All believers who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoyce in Jesus Christ are by the Apostle determined, <ns0:hi>the Cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumcision, Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.3. and he is a <ns0:hi>Iew</ns0:hi> who is one inwardly, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.29. <ns0:hi>And of his Kingdom shall be no end,</ns0:hi> this both expounds the Words <ns0:hi>for ever,</ns0:hi> going just before, and also distinguisheth the Kingdom of Christ, from all Kingdoms of the World, which all shall have their Periods, and also assureth us of the continuance of the Gospel Church, which is Christs Kingdom, till his Kingdom of Glory be revealed, and this agreeth with the Prophecies, of the old Testament, concerning the Kingdom of the Me<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>siah, and the typical Kingdom of <ns0:hi>David, Psal.</ns0:hi> 145.14. <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 9.7. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 7.14. <ns0:hi>Micah</ns0:hi> 4.7.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
